title: Oscar Wilde's London
source_book: Wolf Von Eckardt, Sander L. Gilman and J. Edward Chamberlin, Oscar Wilde's London: A Scrapbook of Vices and Virtues, 1880–1900 (Garden City, NY: Anchor Press/Doubleday, 1987).

themes.name: Wilde's footsteps
themes.summary: Wilde's London was a westward arc, from rooms off the Strand to a house in Chelsea, with a daily round through Piccadilly, St James's and the West End theatres. In 1895 the same map turned into a route through police courts and prisons.
text: He arrived in the autumn of 1879 and took rooms with the painter Frank Miles at 13 Salisbury Street, a lane running down from the Strand to the river, among the theatres and a short walk from the newspapers of Fleet Street. Within a year the two men had moved west to Tite Street in Chelsea, where Whistler, Godwin and Sargent were building and painting beside the Thames. Wilde married Constance Lloyd in 1884 at St James's, Sussex Gardens, near her family's home at Lancaster Gate in Bayswater, and the couple settled at 16 Tite Street, his home until 1895. His mother lived nearby in Oakley Street. From Chelsea his day ran east: the Café Royal on Regent Street, the clubs and hotels of St James's and Albemarle Street, and the St James's and Haymarket theatres, where his four society comedies opened between 1892 and 1895.

In the spring of 1895 the map turns inside out. The card the Marquess of Queensberry left at the Albemarle Club led to Queensberry's committal at Marlborough Street police court and to the libel trial at the Old Bailey. Wilde was then arrested at the Cadogan Hotel, charged at Bow Street and held on remand in Holloway. After the two criminal trials he went to Pentonville and Wandsworth, and in November he stood in convict dress on the platform at Clapham Junction on his way to Reading. These were the institutions on the city's edge, far from the West End front doors he knew. On 19 May 1897 he walked out of Pentonville to Stewart Headlam's house in Bloomsbury, and that night he took the boat to Dieppe.

themes.name: Queer London
themes.source_chapters: Chapter 12, 'Juliets of a Night' (pp. 238–261), with the histories of queer London in the bibliography
themes.summary: Queer London had a geography before it had a name: the promenades, arcades, restaurants and baths of the West End, all within a walk of Wilde's clubs and theatres, and the courts and newspapers that exposed them.
text: Men who desired men met in plain sight. The colonnade of the Quadrant on Regent Street, Piccadilly, Burlington Arcade, the promenade of the Empire in Leicester Square and the paths of Hyde Park near the Knightsbridge Barracks, where guardsmen made extra money, were all known meeting grounds. The Jermyn Street Turkish bath was a male world of its own. The 1895 trials gave this map its best-known addresses: the private rooms of Kettner's and the Solferino in Soho, where Alfred Taylor introduced Wilde to young men, the Savoy and Albemarle hotels, and Taylor's curtained rooms in Little College Street, behind Westminster Abbey.

The layer also traces how the law closed in. Ernest Boulton and Frederick Park were arrested in women's dress at the Strand Theatre in 1870. The painter Simeon Solomon was arrested off Oxford Street in 1873. The Cleveland Street scandal of 1889 ran from a house in Fitzrovia to the Central Telegraph Office in the City and the Marlborough Club on Pall Mall. In 1885 Parliament had passed the Labouchère amendment, which made any 'gross indecency' between men a crime, in public or in private, and which was used to convict Wilde. After 1895 queer London went quieter: in 1897 George Ives founded the secret Order of Chaeronea from Primrose Hill. Women's networks, such as the poet Amy Levy's in Bloomsbury, left fainter traces on the map.

themes.name: Stage & song
themes.source_chapters: Chapter 3, 'Call of the Stage' (pp. 54–79), and chapter 9, 'Sounds of London' (pp. 178–199)
themes.summary: London's theatres crowded into about a square mile between the Strand and Leicester Square. Wilde set out to conquer them, and he was competing with the music halls for the same evening crowds.
text: The Strand and the streets off it held the Lyceum, where Henry Irving and Ellen Terry played Shakespeare and melodrama; the Gaiety, home of burlesque and then of musical comedy; and the Savoy, built for Gilbert and Sullivan and the first public building in London lit entirely by electricity (1881). Patience, the opera that mocked Wilde's Aestheticism in 1881, ran at the Opera Comique nearby. West of Charing Cross, society drama gathered at the St James's and the Haymarket, where Wilde's comedies opened. The new Shaftesbury Avenue and Charing Cross Road added more theatres at the end of the 1880s, among them the Palace, where Salome was banned in rehearsal in 1892. Ibsen arrived at small houses on the margins: A Doll's House at the Novelty in Great Queen Street, Ghosts at the Royalty in Soho.

Around Leicester Square the Alhambra and the Empire offered ballet and variety, and in their promenades a good deal more. Further out, the music halls served their own neighbourhoods: the Canterbury in Lambeth, the first building designed as a music hall (1852); Sadler's Wells in Clerkenwell; and Emma Cons's temperance music hall at the Old Vic. On the map the West End's stalls and the working-class halls are a short walk apart, and Wilde's first nights shared the city with Dan Leno and Marie Lloyd.

themes.name: Art & Aestheticism
themes.summary: Aestheticism lived in the west of the city. The artists lived in Chelsea and Kensington, and the galleries and shops that sold the look to everyone else were on Bond Street, Regent Street and Oxford Street.
text: Chelsea's riverside was the movement's home. Rossetti and Swinburne lived at Tudor House on Cheyne Walk and Carlyle in Cheyne Row. Whistler painted the river from Lindsey Row, turning old Battersea Bridge and the fireworks at Cremorne into nocturnes. Godwin built Whistler the White House in Tite Street, and Wilde followed them into the street. In Kensington and Holland Park, successful painters built studio palaces, such as Leighton's house with its Arab Hall. In Prince's Gate, Whistler painted the Peacock Room for the shipowner Frederick Leyland. The South Kensington Museum served as the nation's school of design.

The West End was where Aestheticism became a style anyone could buy. The Grosvenor Gallery on New Bond Street showed Burne-Jones and Whistler from 1877, and Wilde reviewed its opening exhibition as an undergraduate. Liberty's on Regent Street sold the fabrics and the blue-and-white china, and Morris & Co. kept a showroom on Oxford Street. The suburbs built the look in red brick at Bedford Park, the first garden suburb, at Turnham Green. Upriver at Hammersmith, William Morris joined art to socialism at Kelmscott House. Nothing in this layer lies east of St Paul's.

themes.name: Readers & writers
themes.summary: Literary London ran along one line, the Strand and Fleet Street, from the publishers of the West End to the presses of Ludgate Hill. In the 1890s the newest writing moved west, to Vigo Street and Bloomsbury.
text: Wilde made his living from print long before his plays paid. He reviewed for the Pall Mall Gazette, whose offices stood just off the Strand. From 1887 to 1889 he edited The Woman's World for Cassell's at La Belle Sauvage on Ludgate Hill. He published The Picture of Dorian Gray as a book with Ward, Lock, off Fleet Street. Fleet Street was the newspaper industry's own street, and in Wine Office Court the Cheshire Cheese was where Yeats, Dowson, Lionel Johnson and the Rhymers' Club read their poems to each other. The Strand had the bookshops, and Holywell Street behind it had the trade in pornography.

In the 1890s the new literature moved west. John Lane and Elkin Mathews's Bodley Head in Vigo Street, off Regent Street, published Wilde's Salome and The Sphinx, and then The Yellow Book. Leonard Smithers sold decadence and erotica from the Royal Arcade off Bond Street. Bloomsbury supplied the readers and the New Women writers: the British Museum Reading Room was where Amy Levy, Eleanor Marx and Bernard Shaw worked. The new Charing Cross Road, opened in 1887, filled with secondhand booksellers. Reading this layer from east to west traces the shift from Victorian journalism to the little magazines of the fin de siècle.

themes.name: The growing city
themes.summary: Between 1879 and 1897 London rebuilt itself, with new streets, new railways under and over the ground, and suburbs for the millions who could now travel to work. This layer shows how the places in the other themes were joined up, and how fast they were changing.
text: Wilde's London was a building site. The Victoria Embankment (1870) and the Chelsea Embankment (1874) walled in the Thames and carried Bazalgette's new sewers. Shaftesbury Avenue and Charing Cross Road were driven through the slums of St Giles and Soho in the late 1880s, and Northumberland Avenue filled with six-hundred-room hotels. Electric light came to the Savoy Theatre in 1881. Tower Bridge, opened in 1894, wrapped modern steel in Gothic stone. In 1889 the new London County Council gave the metropolis its first elected government.

Transport redrew the map. The Metropolitan Railway (1863) had opened the first underground line, and the Cheap Trains Act of 1883 required cheap workmen's fares, which carried working families out to new suburbs like Walthamstow and Tottenham. In 1890 the City and South London Railway opened the world's first deep electric tube, running from the City to Stockwell. The middle classes shopped at the new department stores, Whiteley's in Bayswater (where Wilde himself shopped) and Harrods in Knightsbridge. The ceremonial heart of the city, from Trafalgar Square to Buckingham Palace and Westminster Abbey, staged Victoria's two Jubilees, in 1887 and 1897.

themes.name: London's shame
themes.source_chapters: Chapter 6, '…And London's Shame' (pp. 126–145), and chapter 7, 'The Lower Classes' (pp. 146–166)
themes.summary: Slums lay a few hundred yards behind the West End's theatres. Two miles east was a city of docks, sweatshops and lodging houses, which the West End discovered with horror in the 1880s.
text: Poverty was not only an East End matter. Seven Dials and Bedfordbury sat directly behind the theatres of Covent Garden, Lisson Grove behind Marylebone, and Fore Street in Lambeth across the river from Westminster. But the East End, from Whitechapel and Spitalfields to the docks at Poplar, became the great subject of the period. George Sims's How the Poor Live and Andrew Mearns's The Bitter Cry of Outcast London both appeared in 1883, and Charles Booth's survey coloured London street by street from wealth to want. Then came the Whitechapel murders of 1888, which turned these streets into a national spectacle.

The map also shows the responses. Jewish refugees from Eastern Europe landed at the river stairs and found shelter in Leman Street. From 1884 Toynbee Hall in Commercial Street brought university men to live among the poor, and from 1887 the People's Palace on the Mile End Road offered concerts and a library. Dr Barnardo photographed the children he took in at Stepney. Workers organised: the matchgirls struck at Bryant & May in Bow in 1888 and the dockers in 1889. In 1891 Wilde published his own answer, The Soul of Man under Socialism. The new London County Council cleared the Old Nichol in Shoreditch and built its first great housing estate on the site.

themes.name: Juliets of a night
themes.summary: After dark the most fashionable streets in London became its most notorious market for sex. How that market was policed, and how it was reported, set the terms for Wilde's own prosecution.
text: The guidebooks of the day, as the book shows, found 'Juliets of a night' all over the city. They were in Bond Street and Burlington Arcade; in the Haymarket, which smelled of hay by day; on the Strand; in the promenades of the Empire and the Alhambra; and down at the docks along the Ratcliffe Highway. Prostitution was the city's open secret, and it occupied the same West End streets as the theatres, restaurants and clubs. Contemporary estimates of the numbers involved ran as high as 80,000 women, and the figures themselves were weapons in moral campaigns.

In July 1885 W. T. Stead's 'Maiden Tribute of Modern Babylon' in the Pall Mall Gazette described the purchase of a thirteen-year-old girl in Marylebone. The outcry pushed through the Criminal Law Amendment Act, which raised the age of consent to sixteen and, through the Labouchère amendment, also criminalised sex between men. In 1888 the Whitechapel murders turned the poorest women of Spitalfields into a national spectacle. A year later the Cleveland Street scandal showed how the same laws, the same police and the same newspapers would treat men.

themes.name: Pleasures & sport
themes.source_chapters: Chapter 10, 'Virtues of Sport' (pp. 200–218), and chapter 11, 'Jumbo and Sundry Diversions' (pp. 219–237)
themes.summary: Leisure had its own map. Clubs and restaurants filled St James's and the West End, while sport and mass entertainment went to the parks and suburbs, often at the end of a railway line.
text: For a man of Wilde's set, pleasure meant St James's. There was clubland along Pall Mall and St James's Street, and the Marlborough Club for the Prince of Wales's circle. For dinner there were the Café Royal, Kettner's and Romano's. The Pelican Club in Gerrard Street, where Queensberry boxed, gave way in 1891 to the National Sporting Club in Covent Garden, which made prize-fighting respectable under the rules that bore Queensberry's name. Rotten Row in Hyde Park was the Season's parade ground for horses, carriages and courtesans, and in 1895 it filled with bicycles.

Sport and spectacle moved out along the railways and omnibus routes. W. G. Grace drew crowds to Lord's in St John's Wood, Test cricket came to the Oval in Kennington, lawn tennis began at Wimbledon in 1877, and the Boat Race started from Putney. Excursion trains carried crowds to the Crystal Palace at Sydenham, and omnibuses took families to the Zoo in Regent's Park, where the sale of Jumbo the elephant to Barnum in 1882 caused a national uproar. Wilde stood for aesthetics against athletics, a contrast the cartoonists enjoyed. Queensberry's world of the ring and the turf ran through the same streets, and it would bring him down.

themes.name: Religion & spirits
themes.summary: The Church of England had lost the poor. London filled the gap with giant chapels, street armies, settlements, séances and Theosophy, each with its own corner of the map.
text: Westminster Abbey and St Paul's staged the rituals of state, including Victoria's Jubilee services of 1887 and 1897, but the religious energy of the period lay elsewhere. South of the river, Charles Spurgeon preached to congregations of some six thousand at the Metropolitan Tabernacle by the Elephant and Castle. From headquarters in Queen Victoria Street, William Booth's Salvation Army marched with brass bands into the East End. Hawksmoor's Christ Church in Spitalfields stood among the lodging houses, where the homeless slept on the churchyard seats, and Barnardo ran his homes in Stepney.

The western and northern suburbs had their own seekers. Madame Blavatsky's Theosophical Society made its London headquarters at Annie Besant's house in Avenue Road, St John's Wood. Constance Wilde joined the Society, and Gandhi, a law student at the Inner Temple, met Blavatsky and Besant in London. Spiritualist séances were held in middle-class drawing rooms. Wilde's own path led to the Catholic Church: on the day of his release in 1897 he wrote to the Jesuits at Farm Street in Mayfair asking to make a retreat, and was refused. He was received into the Church on his deathbed in Paris in 1900.

places.name: 13 Salisbury Street
places.address: Salisbury Street, off the Strand (demolished; site near Shell Mex House)
places.summary: Wilde's first London rooms, shared with the painter Frank Miles in the autumn of 1879.
text: The authors open their book at this address. In the fall of 1879, fresh from Oxford with a first in Greats and the Newdigate Prize, Wilde took rooms here with his Oxford friend Frank Miles, a fashionable portraitist of society beauties. The house, called Thames House, stood in a narrow street sloping from the Strand down to the river, a district the book calls fashionable at the time.

Miles was sketching Lillie Langtry and other 'professional beauties', and through his studio Wilde met them all. He had little money, sold a poem now and then, and set about making his own life a work of art. The book's whole frame, from 1879 to 1897, runs from this house to Pentonville.
events: Wilde and Frank Miles take rooms at 13 Salisbury Street.

places.name: 1 Tite Street (Keats House)
places.address: 1 Tite Street, now 44 Tite Street, Chelsea
places.summary: Frank Miles's Godwin-designed studio house, where Wilde lodged in 1880–81 and met London society.
text: E. W. Godwin designed this studio house for Frank Miles, and the book reproduces his drawing of its Aesthetic, 'vegetable' facade, much modified before it was built. Miles and Wilde moved here from Salisbury Street in 1880, and Wilde named the house after Keats.

Here the young aesthete received the beauties Miles painted, including Lillie Langtry, and prepared his first volume, Poems (1881). The arrangement ended in 1881, after Miles's father objected to the book's sensuality. Three years later Wilde was back on the same street, at No. 16, as a married man. The book notes that the street sat in a district of artists' studios, with Chelsea's slums close by.
events: Wilde and Miles move to Tite Street.
Wilde leaves Miles's house after the row over Poems.

places.name: 16 Tite Street: the Wildes' house
places.address: 16 Tite Street, now 34 Tite Street, Chelsea (blue plaque)
places.summary: Oscar and Constance Wilde's 'House Beautiful', decorated by Godwin, and auctioned off while Wilde awaited trial.
text: After their marriage in May 1884 the Wildes took this narrow red-brick 'Queen Anne' row house and, with Constance's allowance from her grandfather, had Godwin (helped by Whistler) transform it. The book walks through it: Wilde's red-and-yellow study on the ground floor, with a cast of the Hermes of Praxiteles, a Simeon Solomon, a Monticelli, Beardsley's drawing of Mrs Patrick Campbell and Thomas Carlyle's writing desk. Upstairs was a white drawing room, then bedrooms and nurseries for Cyril (born 1885) and Vyvyan (1886).

Guests included John Bright, Arthur Balfour, Browning, Swinburne, Mark Twain, Ellen Terry, Sarah Bernhardt and Lillie Langtry. In 1891 Lionel Johnson brought Lord Alfred Douglas to tea here, and in June 1894 the Marquess of Queensberry came to the door to threaten Wilde in person. The book points out that Justice Wills, who would sentence him, lived on the same street.

On 24 April 1895, with Wilde in Holloway, the bailiffs held a chaotic sale of the contents to satisfy his creditors. Pictures, manuscripts, presentation copies and the boys' toys went for almost nothing, and souvenir hunters carried off what they could.
events: Oscar and Constance move in after their honeymoon.
Lionel Johnson brings Lord Alfred Douglas to meet Wilde.
Queensberry confronts Wilde in his own house.

places.name: The White House (Whistler's house)
places.summary: Godwin's radical white-brick house for Whistler, lost to bankruptcy after the Ruskin trial.
text: Godwin designed this severe, asymmetrical house with a green slate roof for Whistler in 1877–78. The Metropolitan Board of Works disliked its plainness and forced changes. The book mentions it as an example of Godwin's Japanese-influenced work.

Whistler had barely moved in when the Ruskin libel trial ruined him. He won a farthing in damages, went bankrupt in 1879, and the house was sold. The street became an artists' colony: Whistler kept studios nearby, John Singer Sargent worked there, and in 1884 the Wildes arrived at No. 16.
events: Whistler moves into Godwin's White House.

places.name: 9 Charles Street, Mayfair
places.summary: Wilde's bachelor lodgings after America and Paris, where he lived during his engagement.
text: Back from his American lecture tour and from Paris (where, the book notes, he met Hugo, Verlaine, Zola and Mallarmé), Wilde took rooms here in 1883. He lectured round the provinces on his 'Impressions of America' and on house decoration, and courted Constance Lloyd, who lived across the park at Lancaster Gate.
The address is a reminder that between 1879 and 1884 Wilde lived in lodgings, borrowed rooms and other people's houses. He had a West End address but very little money.

places.name: 100 Lancaster Gate
places.summary: Home of Constance Lloyd's grandfather, where Wilde courted the woman he married.
text: Constance Mary Lloyd lived here with her grandfather, the barrister John Horatio Lloyd. Her allowance from him paid for the decoration of Tite Street, as the book records. Wilde first called on her in 1881 and they became engaged in Dublin in November 1883.

Constance was not only Wilde's wife. She took up the causes of the day, including the Rational Dress Society and Liberal women's politics, and the book notes that she joined the Theosophical Society. Her biographer Franny Moyle has made the case for her as an independent figure.

places.name: St James's Church, Sussex Gardens
places.summary: Where Oscar Wilde married Constance Lloyd on 29 May 1884.
text: The parish church of the Lloyds' Bayswater neighbourhood. The wedding on 29 May 1884 drew a crowd of the curious; the press reported Constance's dress, designed with Wilde's input. After a Paris honeymoon the couple moved into Tite Street.
The book dates the move and the marriage to May 1884, the start of what it treats as Wilde's settled, prosperous decade.

places.name: 1 Ovington Square
places.summary: Lady Wilde ('Speranza') and Willie Wilde's first London home.
text: The book notes that Oscar's elder brother Willie was already in London as a journalist and that their widowed mother had followed him, hoping to recreate the literary salon she had kept in Dublin. Jane Francesca Wilde, the nationalist poet 'Speranza', held Saturday receptions here, in dim rooms crowded with writers, actors and the hopeful.

The Wildes were Irish arrivals in a city the book describes as home to more Irishmen than Dublin. Lady Wilde's salons gave Oscar an early London platform, but the family was never secure and was always short of money.
events: Lady Wilde and Willie settle in Knightsbridge.

places.name: 146 Oakley Street
places.summary: Lady Wilde's last home. Oscar took refuge here, 'a wounded stag', when hotels turned him away on bail.
text: Lady Wilde moved here with Willie in 1887, a short walk from Oscar's house in Tite Street. On 7 May 1895, released on bail between his trials, Wilde was hounded from hotel to hotel by Queensberry's men until he arrived here late at night, exhausted. Willie said he had come like a wounded stag.

Lady Wilde urged him not to flee: if he stayed, even if he went to prison, she said, he would always be her son. She died here in February 1896 while he was in Reading Gaol. The prison authorities refused his request to visit her.
events: Lady Wilde moves to Oakley Street.
Wilde, on bail, takes refuge with his mother and brother.

places.name: Grosvenor Gallery
places.summary: Sir Coutts Lindsay's 'greenery-yallery' gallery, home of Aestheticism, which Wilde reviewed as an undergraduate.
text: Opened in 1877 as an alternative to the Royal Academy, the Grosvenor showed Burne-Jones, Whistler and the painters of the Aesthetic movement. Wilde, still at Oxford, wrote a long review of the first exhibition and wore a coat cut like a cello to the private view.

By 1881 the gallery stood for the whole Aesthetic craze. Gilbert's 'greenery-yallery, Grosvenor Gallery, foot-in-the-grave young man' in Patience pointed straight at it, and the book quotes Labouchère's Truth calling Ellen Terry the actress the Grosvenor age 'must necessarily adore'. Whistler's Nocturne in Black and Gold, the painting that started the Ruskin trial, hung here in 1877.
events: Grosvenor Gallery opens; Whistler's nocturnes provoke Ruskin.
Patience mocks the 'Grosvenor Gallery' young man.

places.name: Royal Academy, Burlington House
places.summary: Every May the Academy's summer exhibition opened the Season, and in 1881 Frith painted Wilde holding court at its private view.
text: The book lists the Royal Academy exhibitions among the fixtures of the London Season. W. P. Frith's satirical painting A Private View at the Royal Academy, 1881 puts Wilde at its centre, lecturing a cluster of admirers on art while Gladstone, Browning, Trollope and Lillie Langtry look on. Frith said he meant to mock the 'craze for aestheticism'.

The book reproduces a similar scene, The Private View from the World's 1882 Christmas issue, with Wilde leaning on his elbow in the corner, Whistler near him and the Prince of Wales at the centre. For a young man with one slim book of poems, Wilde had made himself remarkably easy to recognise.
events: Wilde at the Academy private view, as painted by Frith.

places.name: Opera Comique: Patience
places.address: Strand / Wych Street (demolished 1902; site under Aldwych)
places.summary: The ramshackle 'theatre in a tunnel' where Gilbert and Sullivan's Patience, the great satire of Aestheticism, opened in April 1881.
text: Reached by underground passages from the Strand, the Opera Comique housed the first four Gilbert and Sullivan operas, as the book notes: The Sorcerer, H.M.S. Pinafore, The Pirates of Penzance and Patience. Patience opened on 23 April 1881. Its poet Bunthorne, 'a most intense young man', was taken by the public as Wilde (and by others as Swinburne or Whistler).

The book argues that Patience fixed the middle-class image of Aestheticism, and that D'Oyly Carte spotted its publicity value. He sent Wilde to America in 1882 as a living advertisement for the New York production. Wilde turned the joke into a career.
events: Patience opens at the Opera Comique.

places.name: Adelphi Theatre: Vera cancelled
places.summary: Wilde's first play, Vera, or the Nihilists, was announced here for December 1881 and quietly withdrawn.
text: Wilde's melodrama of Russian revolutionaries was due at the Adelphi in December 1881. After the assassination of Tsar Alexander II that year, and with a Danish-born princess of Wales whose sister was the new Tsarina, the production was dropped. The play reached the stage only in New York in 1883, where it failed.

The book is unsparing about Vera and The Duchess of Padua. It calls them old-fashioned melodramas in stilted, oratorical language, and says Wilde needed another decade to find 'the key to the theater of his day'. He sent Ellen Terry a copy of Vera bound with her name stamped in gold.
events: Vera withdrawn before its London premiere.

places.name: Prince's Hall, Piccadilly
places.address: 190–195 Piccadilly (Royal Institute of Painters in Water Colours building)
places.summary: Hall of the Royal Institute of Painters in Water Colours, where Wilde lectured on America and Whistler gave his 'Ten O'Clock'.
text: Wilde gave his first London lecture on his 'Impressions of America' here in July 1883. In 1883 the hall also housed the Rational Dress Society's exhibition, a cause close to Constance and, later, to Wilde as editor of The Woman's World.

On 20 February 1885 Whistler gave his 'Ten O'Clock' lecture here, so called because it began late enough not to spoil dinner. It was a manifesto for art for art's sake and a barely veiled attack on Wilde. Wilde reviewed it, admiringly and mischievously, in the Pall Mall Gazette. The book quotes their sniping in the World: 'A poor thing, Oscar—but for once, I suppose, your own.'
events: Wilde lectures on his Impressions of America.

places.name: Cassell & Co.: The Woman's World
places.address: La Belle Sauvage Yard, Ludgate Hill (destroyed 1941)
places.summary: Wilde's only salaried job: editor of Cassell's magazine The Woman's World, 1887–89.
text: From 1887 Wilde went to Cassell's offices off Ludgate Hill two or three mornings a week to edit The Lady's World, which he renamed The Woman's World and turned into a magazine of women's opinion as well as fashion. He commissioned work from women writers, including Amy Levy, Olive Schreiner and Marie Corelli, and wrote his own 'Literary and Other Notes'.

The book quotes his praise there for the working dress of the London milkwoman and the North-Country factory girl: 'only the idle classes who dress badly'. It is evidence of a practical, reforming side to Wilde's Aestheticism.
events: First issue of The Woman's World under Wilde.

places.name: The Langham Hotel
places.summary: Scene of the 1889 dinner that produced both The Picture of Dorian Gray and The Sign of Four.
text: On 30 August 1889 J. M. Stoddart, managing editor of the Philadelphia monthly Lippincott's, gave a dinner here for Arthur Conan Doyle and Oscar Wilde. The book tells the story from Doyle's side. It was 'a golden evening' for him, because Wilde had read and admired Micah Clarke.

Both men promised Stoddart a story. Doyle delivered The Sign of the Four, Sherlock Holmes's second case, and Wilde The Picture of Dorian Gray, published in Lippincott's in July 1890. The book places the dinner among the 'carefully arranged' literary encounters of Wilde's London. The hotel is not named in the book. The venue comes from the biographies.
events: Stoddart's dinner for Wilde and Conan Doyle.

places.name: Ward, Lock & Co.
places.address: Warwick House, Salisbury Square, off Fleet Street
places.summary: London publishers of Lippincott's Monthly, and of Dorian Gray in book form in 1891.
text: Ward, Lock distributed Lippincott's in Britain, so the July 1890 Dorian Gray went out from Salisbury Square. The reviews were savage. The book quotes Charles Whibley in Henley's Scots Observer asking 'Why go grubbing in muck heaps?' and calling the novel's interest 'medico-legal', and another reviewer sneering that Wilde wrote for 'outlawed noblemen and perverted telegraph boys', an allusion to Cleveland Street.

Wilde answered in letters to the papers and in the famous preface, published in the expanded book edition of April 1891: 'There is no such thing as a moral or an immoral book.' The book notes that the attacks prefigured the case made against him in court.
events: Revised Dorian Gray published in book form.

images.caption: Lippincott's Monthly Magazine, July 1890, with The Picture of Dorian Gray
images.author: Unknown author

places.name: Osgood, McIlvaine & Co.
places.summary: Publishers of Wilde's annus mirabilis of 1891: Intentions, Lord Arthur Savile's Crime and A House of Pomegranates.
text: In a single year this Albemarle Street firm brought out Intentions (with 'The Decay of Lying' and 'The Critic as Artist'), the story collection Lord Arthur Savile's Crime and the fairy tales A House of Pomegranates. The book quotes from all three. Its pages on Covent Garden at dawn come from 'Lord Arthur Savile's Crime', and its thoughts on Chopin from 'The Critic as Artist'.
Albemarle Street was Wilde's corner of Mayfair. His club, the Albemarle, the hotel where he stayed in 1892, and Queensberry's hotel were all within a few doors.
events: Intentions, Lord Arthur Savile's Crime and A House of Pomegranates published.

places.name: David Bogue: Poems (1881)
places.summary: Publisher of Wilde's first book, Poems, printed at the author's expense in 1881.
text: Wilde paid for the printing of Poems, published by Bogue in June 1881. It sold respectably and went through several editions, but critics mocked it and the Oxford Union refused a presented copy as derivative.

Beerbohm, quoted by the book, called the volume a kind of 'decoy to the shy artificers of Chelsea'. It was a way into the world of Rossetti, Swinburne and Whistler. The book reprints 'Impression du Matin', Wilde's Whistlerian Thames nocturne, and finds it 'at once precious in its romanticism and precise in its realism'.

images.caption: Oscar Wilde, photographed by Elliott & Fry, 1881
images.author: Elliott & Fry

places.name: St James's Theatre
places.summary: George Alexander's theatre: Lady Windermere's Fan (1892) and The Importance of Being Earnest (1895).
text: Under Hare and the Kendals in the 1880s the St James's staged Pinero's early plays, and the book tells of the 1881 row over whether Pinero's The Squire had lifted its plot from Hardy's Far from the Madding Crowd. Under George Alexander it became the home of the well-made society play: Pinero's The Second Mrs Tanqueray (1893), with Mrs Patrick Campbell, and Wilde's comedies.

Lady Windermere's Fan opened here on 20 February 1892, with Wilde's curtain speech congratulating the audience on its good taste. Henry James's Guy Domville flopped here in January 1895 and was replaced by The Importance of Being Earnest on 14 February 1895. The book quotes Allan Aynesworth, the first Algernon: in 53 years of acting he never remembered 'a greater triumph'.

That night Queensberry tried to get in with a bouquet of carrots and turnips. Police turned him away. Weeks later, as the scandal broke, Wilde's name was pasted over on the playbills, and the play soon came off.
events: Pinero's The Second Mrs Tanqueray opens.
The Importance of Being Earnest opens; Queensberry barred.
Wilde's name removed from the bills.

images.caption: Playbill for The Importance of Being Earnest, St James's Theatre, 1895
images.author: Unknown author

images.author: Unknown author

places.name: Theatre Royal, Haymarket
places.summary: The Bancrofts' house, where Lillie Langtry debuted in 1881, and where Wilde's A Woman of No Importance and An Ideal Husband opened.
text: The Bancrofts took over the Haymarket in 1880 and had it remodelled. The book describes how abolishing the cheap pit for expensive stalls set off a protest that held up the first night for twenty minutes. Lillie Langtry made her stage debut here in She Stoops to Conquer in December 1881. The book links her new career to the Prince of Wales's persuading his mother back to the theatre.

Under Herbert Beerbohm Tree, A Woman of No Importance opened here on 19 April 1893. An Ideal Husband followed on 3 January 1895, with the Prince of Wales in the royal box. The book quotes his advice to Wilde about cuts: 'Cut not a single word.'
events: A Woman of No Importance opens.

images.caption: The Haymarket, with the Theatre Royal
images.author: DimiTalen

places.name: Palace Theatre: Salome banned
places.address: Cambridge Circus (opened 1891 as the Royal English Opera House)
places.summary: Salome, with Sarah Bernhardt, was in rehearsal here when the Lord Chamberlain banned it in June 1892.
text: Wilde wrote Salome in French for Sarah Bernhardt, and rehearsals began in June 1892 in D'Oyly Carte's new opera house at Cambridge Circus. The Lord Chamberlain's Examiner of Plays refused a licence under the old rule against showing biblical characters on stage, and the production collapsed.

Wilde threatened to become a French citizen. The play appeared in print instead, in French in 1893 and in English in 1894 with Beardsley's drawings, in a translation by Lord Alfred Douglas that Wilde heavily corrected. The book reproduces Beardsley's illustrations and Wilde's complaint that they were 'too Japanese, while my play is Byzantine'. One of them caricatures Wilde's face.

places.name: 10–11 St James's Place
places.address: St James's Place, off St James's Street
places.summary: The rooms Wilde rented to write in, 1893–94, where An Ideal Husband took shape.
text: From October 1893 Wilde kept rooms here, a short walk from his clubs, the St James's Theatre and the Haymarket. He came most mornings to write and worked on An Ideal Husband here.

The arrangement suited a double life: a family home in Chelsea and a set of rooms in clubland. Under cross-examination in April 1895 Wilde himself dated the chambers from October 1893 to April 1894. Visits by young men to these rooms were part of the case against him.
events: Wilde takes rooms in St James's Place.

places.name: Café Royal
places.summary: The gilded Domino Room was Wilde and Bosie's daily haunt in the early 1890s, and where Frank Harris begged Wilde to flee.
text: The book counts the Café Royal among the café-restaurants of Wilde's London, with Verrey's, Gatti's and Romano's, and says Wilde and Lord Alfred Douglas frequented it in the early 1890s. It quotes Max Beerbohm's description of the Domino Room, all gilding, crimson velvet, mirrors and caryatids under a painted ceiling, with dominoes clattering on marble tables: 'This indeed is life!'

William Rothenstein, whose sketch of the ageing Wilde the book reproduces, belonged to the circle of artists and writers who met here. In late March 1895, at lunch here with Bernard Shaw present, Frank Harris told Wilde he would lose the libel action and urged him to go abroad. Douglas arrived and pushed him on.
events: Frank Harris urges Wilde, at lunch here, to abandon the case.

images.caption: William Orpen, The Café Royal, London, 1912
images.author: William Orpen

places.name: Kettner's
places.summary: The Soho restaurant where, by Wilde's own testimony, Alfred Taylor introduced him to Charles and William Parker.
text: The book explains that the drinking places of the upper classes were 'places of assignation', and that the trial testimony placed Wilde's meetings with working-class youths not in pubs but in Soho restaurants with private dining rooms.

Contemporary reports of the libel trial have Wilde telling Carson that he first met Charles Parker at Kettner's, at a dinner for Alfred Taylor's birthday to which Taylor brought the two Parker brothers. Carson's question, whether the wine was Kettner's best, got a laugh in court. William Parker repeated the Kettner's version at the second criminal trial. The book instead quotes Charles Parker naming the Solferino in Rupert Street (see that entry), so the sources disagree on where the dinner took place.
In 1898, the book adds, Soho had one drinking house for every two hundred people.
events: Wilde tells the court he first met Charles Parker at Kettner's.

places.name: The Solferino, Rupert Street
places.summary: In the testimony the book prints, Charles Parker names the Solferino as the place where Taylor introduced him to Wilde. Other reports name Kettner's.
text: The book prints part of Charles Parker's evidence at the 1895 trials. Parker, an unemployed valet, said Alfred Taylor took him and his brother William to a restaurant in Rupert Street, 'I think it was the Solferino', and up to a private room with dinner laid for four. Wilde arrived, paid for champagne, brandy and coffee, and afterwards took Parker by cab to the Savoy.

The book uses the episode to show that sex across class lines was organised through the restaurants of Soho. Reports of the libel trial, however, have Wilde (and later William Parker) placing that first dinner at Kettner's, so this marker shows the version the book prints. The disagreement is a reminder that trial testimony, and the reconstructions published decades later, do not always agree.
events: Parker meets Wilde here, by his account.
Parker testifies at the Old Bailey.

places.name: Savoy Hotel
places.summary: D'Oyly Carte's luxury hotel of 1889, where Wilde and Douglas stayed in 1893, as the trials laid bare.
text: Built by Richard D'Oyly Carte beside his theatre and opened in 1889, the Savoy had electric light and lifts, and more bathrooms than any hotel in London. The book describes the new 'monster' hotels catering to 'the idlers of the globe'.

In March 1893 Wilde and Douglas took rooms here. At the trials, chambermaids and a masseur gave evidence about what they had seen, and the prosecution leaned on it heavily. The book reprints Charles Parker's testimony that Wilde took him from the Solferino to his sitting room and bedroom at the Savoy.
events: Wilde and Douglas stay at the Savoy.

images.caption: Oscar Wilde and Lord Alfred Douglas, 1893
images.author: Unknown author

places.name: Albemarle Hotel
places.summary: Wilde stayed here in 1892–93. Edward Shelley, a Bodley Head clerk, testified to visits.
text: Wilde used this hotel at the foot of Albemarle Street in late 1892 and early 1893. Edward Shelley, a young clerk at the Bodley Head (Wilde's publisher), said in 1895 that Wilde had invited him here. Shelley was one of the most damaging and also most fragile witnesses.
The hotel shows how closely Wilde's literary and sexual lives were woven into the same few Mayfair streets.
events: Wilde stays at the Albemarle Hotel.

places.name: Hotel Avondale
places.summary: Wilde's base in February 1895, from which he went to the Albemarle Club and found Queensberry's card.
text: Wilde was staying at the Avondale with Douglas in February 1895, piling up a bill he could not pay. From here he went round to his club on 28 February and was handed Queensberry's card. That night he wrote to Robert Ross that he saw nothing for it but a criminal prosecution.
When Wilde tried to leave the Avondale, the hotel held his luggage against the unpaid bill. It was a small sign of how little money he had for the case he was about to bring.
events: Wilde, staying here, collects Queensberry's card.

places.name: Albemarle Club
places.summary: Where Queensberry left his card 'For Oscar Wilde posing as a somdomite', the start of Wilde's fall.
text: Unusually, the Albemarle admitted women as well as men, and both Oscar and Constance were members. On 18 February 1895 the Marquess of Queensberry, staying at Carter's Hotel a few doors up the street, left his card with the hall porter, scrawled 'For Oscar Wilde posing as somdomite' (his spelling). The porter put it in an envelope, and Wilde received it on 28 February.
The book notes the misspelling twice. On Douglas's urging, Wilde swore out a warrant for criminal libel. Within three months the case had turned into his own prosecution.
events: Queensberry leaves his card at the club.

images.caption: Queensberry's card left for Wilde at the Albemarle Club, 1895 (National Archives, CRIM 1/6)
images.author: The National Archives UK

images.caption: The Marquess of Queensberry by Ape, Vanity Fair, 1877
images.author: Leslie Ward

places.name: Marlborough Street Police Court
places.summary: Queensberry was arrested and charged with criminal libel here on 2 March 1895.
text: On 1 March 1895 Wilde, with Douglas, applied for a warrant. The next day Queensberry was arrested and brought here, then committed for trial at a hearing on 9 March. He filed a plea of justification: the libel was true and published in the public interest.
His solicitors then had private detectives assemble the names of young men connected with Wilde. The book compresses all this into a sentence: Wilde sued, lost and was arrested.

places.name: Central Criminal Court (Old Bailey) and Newgate
places.address: Old Bailey (rebuilt 1902–07 on the site of Newgate Prison)
places.summary: Scene of all three trials: the libel case against Queensberry (3–5 April) and Wilde's two criminal trials (April–May 1895).
text: In the old Sessions House beside Newgate Prison, Edward Carson cross-examined Wilde in the libel trial. Wilde was brilliant on literature, then fatally flippant about a servant boy he had not kissed because he was 'too ugly'. The prosecution withdrew on 5 April and Queensberry was acquitted. The book reproduces the Illustrated Police News's crude strip of the trial: Wilde in the dock beside the renters who testified, his American lecture days, and the sale at Tite Street.

Arrested that evening, Wilde stood trial here with Alfred Taylor from 26 April. The jury failed to agree on 1 May. At a second trial before Mr Justice Wills he was convicted on 25 May 1895 of gross indecency under the 1885 Labouchère amendment and sentenced to two years' hard labour, the maximum. (The book misprints the year as 1889.) The book likens watching the Wilde trials to the public executions abolished a generation earlier. It also reproduces an engraving of a London prison exercise yard, the kind of place the sentence led to.
events: Wilde v. Queensberry: the libel case collapses.
Second trial; Wilde convicted and sentenced to two years' hard labour.

images.caption: The trial of Oscar Wilde and Alfred Taylor, Illustrated Police News, 1895
images.author: Illustrated Police News , a newspaper from the 19th century.

images.caption: Newgate Prison and the Sessions House, drawn by Philip Norman
images.author: Philip Norman

places.name: Holborn Viaduct Hotel
places.summary: Where Wilde retreated with Douglas and Ross on 5 April 1895 after the libel case collapsed, and wrote to the Evening News.
text: Leaving the Old Bailey on the morning of 5 April, Wilde went with Douglas and Robert Ross to this railway hotel a few hundred yards away. There he wrote to the Evening News that he had withdrawn to spare Douglas from appearing in the witness box against his father.

The viaduct itself was a showpiece of mid-Victorian engineering. The book reproduces an advertisement from a neighbouring address for the 'Electropathic Belt', a cure-all sold from 21 Holborn Viaduct.
events: Wilde writes to the Evening News from the hotel.

places.name: Cadogan Hotel
places.summary: Wilde was arrested in Room 118 here on the evening of 5 April 1895.
text: Douglas had rooms here. Through the afternoon of 5 April, while friends urged him to catch the boat train to France, Wilde sat drinking hock and seltzer and did not move. At about 6.30 pm two detectives arrived with a warrant, and he was taken to Scotland Yard and then to Bow Street.

John Betjeman's poem 'The Arrest of Oscar Wilde at the Cadogan Hotel' (1937) made the moment famous. The book points to another escape route: if Wilde had followed Lord Arthur Somerset's example after Cleveland Street, he would never have gone to Reading Gaol.
events: Wilde arrested at the Cadogan Hotel.

places.name: Bow Street Police Court
places.summary: London's chief magistrates' court, where Boulton and Park appeared in 1870 and Wilde was committed for trial in April 1895.
text: Wilde spent the night of his arrest in the cells here. Over the following days, hearings in the crowded courtroom committed him and Alfred Taylor for trial, and bail was refused. Crowds outside jeered.

Bow Street had seen a famous queer case before. In 1870 the cross-dressing young men Ernest Boulton and Frederick Park were brought here in their gowns after their arrest at the Strand Theatre. Their acquittal in 1871 showed how hard sodomy was to prove, and that difficulty is part of why the 1885 'gross indecency' offence mattered so much.
events: Boulton and Park brought before the magistrate.
Wilde charged at Bow Street; bail refused.
Wilde and Taylor committed for trial.

images.caption: Outside Bow Street Magistrates' Court, c. 1908
images.author: Flickr Commons

places.name: Holloway Prison
places.summary: Wilde was held on remand here in April–May 1895, between his arrest and his first trial.
text: Holloway was then a men's as well as a women's prison. Wilde was held here on remand from April 1895. Douglas visited him almost daily until Wilde's friends persuaded him to go abroad before the trial. Wilde wrote of him from here with great tenderness.
While he waited in his cell, the contents of his house in Tite Street were sold.

places.name: St Pancras Station and Midland Grand Hotel
places.summary: Scott's Gothic railway palace, painted in 1884 at sunset, and one of the hotels that turned Wilde away on bail.
text: The book opens with John O'Connor's 1884 painting of St Pancras from Pentonville Road at sunset, horse trams in the damp street. It calls Gilbert Scott's Midland Grand Hotel a 'huge Gothic Revival castle' assembled from no fewer than fifty sketchbooks of ornament. Its 300-foot clock tower was meant to convince the Midland Railway's shareholders of its power.

On 7 May 1895, released on bail, Wilde took a room here. Queensberry's hired men told the management who he was and he was asked to leave. The same happened elsewhere until he ended the night at his mother's house in Oakley Street.
events: O'Connor paints St Pancras at sunset.
Wilde, on bail, is turned out of the hotel.

images.caption: John O'Connor, From Pentonville Road Looking West: Evening, 1884
images.author: John O'Connor

places.name: 2 Courtfield Gardens: the Leversons
places.summary: Ada 'Sphinx' Leverson and her husband gave Wilde shelter here between his trials.
text: The novelist and wit Ada Leverson, Wilde's 'Sphinx', and her husband Ernest took him in when no hotel would have him. They told their servants he could stay or leave as he wished. He spent the weeks before his second trial here, keeping to the nursery floor and dining with the family.
From here he went each day to the Old Bailey in May 1895. On the eve of the verdict, friends again urged him to flee, and again he stayed.
events: Wilde stays with the Leversons before his second trial.

places.name: Pentonville Prison
places.summary: Where Wilde began his sentence in May 1895, and from which he was released on 19 May 1897.
text: Sentenced on 25 May 1895, Wilde was taken here to begin two years' hard labour: the treadmill, picking oakum, a plank bed and enforced silence. The model prison of the 1840s was built on the 'separate system', designed to isolate prisoners from one another. In July he was moved to Wandsworth.

He came back here at the end of his sentence, brought from Reading so that he could be released quietly in London. The book frames all of Wilde's London between two departures: arriving in 1879, and walking out of Pentonville in the spring of 1897 to take the night boat to Dieppe, 'never to return to England'.
events: Wilde begins his sentence at Pentonville.

places.name: Wandsworth Prison
places.summary: Wilde's prison from July to November 1895, where his health broke down.
text: Moved here in July 1895, Wilde suffered from hunger, dysentery and sleeplessness. He collapsed in chapel and injured his ear, an injury that may have contributed to his death five years later. Richard Haldane, a Liberal MP who sat on a prison reform committee, visited him and arranged for him to have books.
On 20 November 1895 he was taken from here to Reading Gaol.

images.caption: Wandsworth Prison (Surrey House of Correction), c. 1860
images.author: Unknown author

places.name: Clapham Junction
places.summary: On 20 November 1895, on his way to Reading, Wilde stood in convict dress on the platform here while a crowd mocked him.
text: Changing trains on the journey from Wandsworth to Reading, Wilde was made to wait on the central platform for half an hour, in convict clothes and handcuffs, in the rain. As word spread, a crowd gathered to laugh, and one man spat at him.

He wrote about it in De Profundis: for a year afterwards he wept every day at the same hour. Clapham Junction, the busiest railway junction in Britain, was a monument of the railway age the book describes. For Wilde it became the place of his worst public humiliation.
events: Wilde mocked on the platform at Clapham Junction.

places.name: Bankruptcy Court, Carey Street
places.address: Bankruptcy Buildings, Carey Street, Lincoln's Inn
places.summary: Wilde was brought here from prison for his bankruptcy examinations in September and November 1895.
text: Queensberry petitioned for Wilde's bankruptcy to recover his costs of some £600. Wilde was brought from Wandsworth for hearings here in September and November 1895. In a corridor, Robert Ross waited to raise his hat as Wilde passed in handcuffs, and Wilde never forgot it.
'Being in Carey Street' was already slang for being bankrupt. The book describes the forced sale at Tite Street that came before these hearings.
events: First bankruptcy examination; Ross raises his hat.

places.name: 31 Upper Bedford Place: Stewart Headlam's house
places.summary: Wilde's first stop as a free man, early on 19 May 1897, at the home of the radical clergyman who had stood bail for him.
text: The Christian Socialist priest Stewart Headlam had put up half of Wilde's bail in 1895, though he barely knew him, on principle. Collected from Pentonville at dawn on 19 May 1897, Wilde came here to change and talk, and wrote asking to go on retreat with the Jesuits. He was refused.
That evening he left for Newhaven and the night boat to Dieppe. He never came back to London.
events: Wilde, freed, spends the day at Headlam's house and leaves for Dieppe.

places.name: Willis's Rooms
places.address: King Street, St James's (site of the former Almack's)
places.summary: Fashionable restaurant in the old Almack's assembly rooms, a favourite of Wilde's in his years of success.
text: The old Almack's Assembly Rooms, once the most exclusive ballroom in Regency London, became Willis's Rooms and in the 1890s a fashionable restaurant. Wilde dined here often when his plays were running at the St James's, a few doors along King Street.
In De Profundis he reckoned what he had spent on dinners and suppers with Douglas in such places. It came to a great deal of money.

images.caption: Almack's Assembly Rooms, later Willis's Rooms, 1821
images.author: George Cruikshank

places.name: 13 Little College Street: Alfred Taylor's rooms
places.summary: Alfred Taylor's curtained, perfumed rooms behind Westminster Abbey, central to the prosecution's case.
text: Alfred Taylor, a public-school man who had run through his inheritance, kept rooms here lit by coloured lamps and heavily curtained, with incense burning. Young men met here, and Taylor introduced several, including the Parker brothers, to Wilde.
Taylor refused to turn Queen's evidence, was tried alongside Wilde and received the same sentence. In the book's account he is the go-between in Charles Parker's testimony.

places.name: 20 Fitzroy Street: the 'Fitzroy settlement'
places.summary: The Century Guild house of Herbert Horne and Arthur Mackmurdo, where Lionel Johnson lived and the Rhymers sometimes met.
text: The book describes the Rhymers' Club, a dozen poets who read their verses aloud in alphabetical order from Dowson to Yeats. It says Wilde came only when they met in a private house. This was one of those houses, the Arts and Crafts household of the Century Guild, where the poet Lionel Johnson had rooms.
Johnson, the book notes, introduced Wilde to Lord Alfred Douglas in 1891. He later wrote a poem, 'The Destroyer of a Soul', that is usually read as aimed at Wilde.
events: Lionel Johnson, of this circle, introduces Wilde to Douglas.

places.name: 19 Cleveland Street
places.summary: The male brothel at the centre of the 1889–90 Cleveland Street scandal, which touched the Prince of Wales's household.
text: The book tells the story in detail. A theft at the Central Telegraph Office led police to a fifteen-year-old messenger, Charles Swinscow, who had more money than his wages explained. He said he earned it 'going to bed with gentlemen' at 19 Cleveland Street. Among the house's visitors were Lord Arthur Somerset, superintendent of the Prince of Wales's stables, and the Earl of Euston. Rumour even named the prince's son, Prince Albert Victor.

The telegraph boys were tried and jailed. Somerset, tipped off, as the book says, by 'someone in Whitehall', escaped to France. When the journalist Ernest Parke printed Euston's name he was convicted of libel and given twelve months. The book sides with Labouchère, who denounced 'one law for a nobleman and another for a man of low estate', and notes that it happened a few months before Dorian Gray appeared.
(The book dates the theft to 4 July 1886. The scandal actually broke in July 1889.)
events: Telegraph boys' visits to 19 Cleveland Street discovered.
Ernest Parke convicted of libelling the Earl of Euston.

images.caption: Cleveland Street scandal in the press, 1890
images.author: Unknown artist (1890)

places.name: Central Telegraph Office (GPO East)
places.summary: The Post Office's telegraph hub, whose uniformed messenger boys were drawn into the Cleveland Street affair.
text: The telegraph was the Victorian internet, and this great building in the City was its exchange, staffed by hundreds of clerks and messenger boys. The book places the start of the Cleveland Street scandal here, with missing money and a messenger boy's unexplained shillings.

The case connected modern communications, a youthful working-class workforce and aristocratic vice. The reviewer the book quotes on Dorian Gray, writing for 'outlawed noblemen and perverted telegraph boys', needed to say nothing more.
events: Investigation begins after a theft here.

places.name: Strand Theatre: Boulton and Park
places.address: Strand, near Surrey Street (demolished 1905; site of Aldwych station)
places.summary: Where the cross-dressing Ernest Boulton and Frederick Park were arrested in April 1870, the most notorious queer case before Wilde's.
text: Ernest Boulton and Frederick Park, known as 'Stella' and 'Fanny', were well-known figures in the West End, sometimes in gowns and sometimes not. They were arrested leaving this theatre in April 1870 and charged with conspiring to commit sodomy. Their trial at Westminster Hall in 1871 ended in acquittal: the prosecution could not prove the act, and dressing as women was not a crime.

Historians such as Morris Kaplan and Charles Upchurch see the case as a turning point. It showed the law's difficulty in convicting men who loved men, and it helps explain why the 'gross indecency' clause of 1885, which needed no proof of sodomy, could catch Wilde. The book does not mention the case. It belongs on this map as the background to his.
events: Boulton and Park arrested at the Strand Theatre.

images.caption: Boulton and Park leaving Bow Street, 1870
images.author: The Illustrated Police News

places.name: Westminster Hall: the old law courts
places.summary: Until 1882 the superior courts sat here: Boulton and Park were acquitted in 1871, and Whistler won his farthing in 1878.
text: Before the Royal Courts of Justice opened in the Strand in 1882, the courts of Queen's Bench, Common Pleas and Exchequer sat in buildings along the side of Westminster Hall. In November 1878 Whistler's libel action against John Ruskin was heard here. The book calls it 'the most curious trial in the annals of the history of art'.

Ruskin had accused Whistler of 'flinging a pot of paint in the public's face'. Asked whether he charged two hundred guineas for two days' work, Whistler replied that he asked it 'for the knowledge of a lifetime'. He won a farthing's damages and went bankrupt. Seven years earlier, in 1871, Boulton and Park had been acquitted in the same courts.

images.caption: Whistler, Nocturne in Black and Gold: The Falling Rocket, 1875
images.author: James McNeill Whistler

places.name: Stratford Place: Simeon Solomon's arrest
places.summary: The Pre-Raphaelite painter Simeon Solomon was arrested in a public urinal here in 1873. His career never recovered.
text: Simeon Solomon, a gifted Jewish painter of the Pre-Raphaelite circle and friend of Swinburne, was arrested in February 1873 with a labourer in a public lavatory near here and convicted of attempted sodomy. Patrons and friends dropped him. He spent much of the rest of his life in poverty and died in the St Giles workhouse in 1905.

Wilde kept faith with his art. The book lists a Simeon Solomon among the few pictures in Wilde's study at Tite Street and reproduces Solomon's 'Winged Thought'. The painting was sold off in the 1895 auction.

images.caption: Simeon Solomon, Sappho and Erinna in a Garden at Mytilene, 1864
images.author: Simeon Solomon

places.name: Turkish Bath, Jermyn Street
places.summary: London's grandest Victorian Turkish bath, a homosocial space that historians of queer London have studied closely.
text: The Hammam on Jermyn Street, opened in 1862, offered steam, massage and Moorish tiles to the men of clubland. Matt Cook shows how Turkish baths figured in late-Victorian queer life as places where male intimacy could pass as health and leisure.

The book does not discuss the baths, but its chapter on clubs and diversions describes the exclusive male institutions of St James's that surrounded them. The baths sat a minute's walk from Wilde's rooms in St James's Place.

images.caption: Section of the Jermyn Street Hammam, 1861
images.author: R A Carter

places.name: Knightsbridge Barracks and the Park
places.summary: Guardsmen supplementing their pay were part of the sexual economy of the Park, as police and diarists recorded.
text: Soldiers of the Household Cavalry and the Foot Guards were notoriously underpaid, and the paths of Hyde Park and St James's Park were known places for men to meet soldiers willing to be paid. Matt Cook and others trace this 'trade' through police records and memoirs.

The book makes a related point about soldiers: it cites a contemporary study claiming that a fifth of the British Army, including the Brigade of Guards, had venereal disease. It is a reminder of the military's place in the city's sexual economy.

images.caption: Hyde Park (Knightsbridge) Barracks today: Basil Spence's 1970 rebuilding on the site of the Victorian cavalry barracks
images.author: Karl1587

places.name: 196 Adelaide Road: George Ives and the Order of Chaeronea
places.summary: Home of George Ives, who founded the secret Order of Chaeronea in 1897, two years after Wilde's conviction.
text: George Cecil Ives, a writer and penal reformer who met Wilde and Douglas in the 1890s, founded the Order of Chaeronea in 1897. It was a secret society for men who loved men, named after the battle where the Sacred Band of Thebes died. It had rituals, a calendar and a commitment to legal reform.

Ives kept a diary for decades and collected press cuttings on sex and crime. Historians have used both to recover a queer London that did not end with Wilde's fall. In some ways it organised in response to it.
events: George Ives founds the Order of Chaeronea.

places.name: 7 Endsleigh Gardens: Amy Levy
places.summary: Home of the poet and novelist Amy Levy, who wrote for Wilde's Woman's World and whose poems addressed women.
text: Amy Levy, the first Jewish woman at Newnham College, Cambridge, wrote London poems (A London Plane-Tree, 1889), the novel Reuben Sachs and love poems to women. She worked in the British Museum Reading Room among the 'New Women' of Bloomsbury. Wilde published her in The Woman's World and wrote an appreciation after her suicide here in September 1889, at twenty-seven.

She is a reminder that queer London was not only male, and that Wilde's editorship gave women writers a platform. The book discusses 'New Woman' writing and the bicycle as liberation; Levy belongs to that world.
events: Amy Levy dies at Endsleigh Gardens.

places.name: Marlborough Club
places.summary: The Prince of Wales's own club, which the book links to the 'Old Boys' Labouchère accused of covering up Cleveland Street.
text: Founded by the Prince of Wales in 1869 after White's refused to let him smoke in the morning room, the Marlborough was the centre of his fast set. The book lists it among London's exclusive clubs.

In its account of Cleveland Street, the book says Labouchère's real target was not the corruption of telegraph boys but 'the corruption of the Old Boys in government and the Marlborough Club, the favorite hangout of Edward, Prince of Wales'.

places.name: Burlington Arcade
places.summary: A luxury Regency shopping arcade with a reputation, after dark, as a place to pick someone up.
text: The book places 'Juliets of a Night' all over town, from 'fashionable Bond Street and Burlington Arcade' to the docks. The arcade's beadles kept order by day, but its upstairs rooms and the crowds of the Piccadilly promenade gave it a double life.

Historians of queer London note that the arcade, like the Quadrant and the Empire promenade, was known for male prostitution too. In 1881 a police superintendent told a House of Lords committee about juveniles arrested for theft from carriages in nearby Bond Street. The respectable West End and the night trade occupied the same few streets.

places.name: The Haymarket by night
places.summary: The street smelled of hay by day and was London's most visible prostitution market by night.
text: The book notes two Haymarkets. By day the old hay market still lent the street its smell. By night it was the best-known place to find a prostitute in the West End. It says as many as half of the women plying their trade in the back streets, 'most visibly on Haymarket', were former domestic servants, dismissed without 'a character' (a reference) after a pregnancy.
When the London Season ended and the dressmakers' girls were laid off, the book says, some 'drifted to Haymarket'. The street links the economics of service and seasonal labour to the night trade.

places.name: Ratcliffe Highway
places.summary: The sailors' high street of the docks, with pubs, dance halls and brothels.
text: The book names Ratcliffe Highway as the chief of the 'red-light districts along the docks'. Sailors paid off from long voyages came ashore here to pubs, music saloons, lodging houses and brothels, many run for and by the polyglot port population the book describes.
Nearby lay the opium rooms of Bluegate Fields. Respectable London visited the district through journalists' sensational accounts, and Dorian Gray goes there to forget.

places.name: Gerrard Street: the Pelican Club and Mother Willit
places.summary: Home of the raffish Pelican Club, where Queensberry boxed, and of a notorious brothel-keeper.
text: The book quotes the bawd 'Mother Willit of Gerrard Street', who boasted that she always turned her girls out 'with a clean arse and good tog'. It uses her to show that the brothel offered what virtue should have provided: food, cleanliness and clothes.

The Pelican Club met on the same street from 1887. It was Bohemian and aristocratic, staged prize fights and numbered the Marquess of Queensberry among its members. The book says it did little to make boxing respectable, and the National Sporting Club replaced it in 1891.
events: The Pelican Club opens in Gerrard Street.
Superseded by the National Sporting Club.

places.name: Holywell Street
places.summary: A crooked lane of overhanging old houses, London's centre of the trade in pornography.
text: Running parallel to the Strand behind St Clement Danes, Holywell Street ('Booksellers' Row') sold second-hand books by day and, under the counter, the erotica the book describes: from The Pearl, a 'Journal of Facetiae and Voluptuous Reading', to photographs. Men went to the Strand or Holywell Street, the book says, 'not for bravery but pornography'.
The street was swept away with the slums around it when Aldwych and Kingsway were cut through in 1900–05. That demolition is the kind of improvement the book's chapter on London's growth describes.

images.author: Philip Norman

images.caption: Booksellers' Row (Holywell Street), drawn by Frank Lewis Emanuel
images.author: Frank Lewis Emanuel

places.name: Savoy Theatre
places.summary: D'Oyly Carte's theatre for Gilbert and Sullivan, the first public building in London lit entirely by electricity (1881).
text: The book opens its theatre chapter here. When the Savoy opened in October 1881 it was lit by some twelve hundred electric lamps fed by six generators. D'Oyly Carte reassured the audience that gas stood by in case the 'experiment' failed. The light changed everything, the book argues: actors now had to look their parts, ladies swapped coloured stones for diamonds, and decoration became more restrained.

Patience transferred here from the Opera Comique, followed by Iolanthe, The Mikado (1885), The Yeomen of the Guard (1888) and The Gondoliers. The book reproduces Alice Havers's 1885 programmes. Queen Victoria never went, but she commanded Savoy operas at Windsor and Balmoral.
events: Savoy Theatre opens, lit by electricity, with Patience.

places.name: Lyceum Theatre
places.summary: Henry Irving and Ellen Terry's temple of Shakespeare and melodrama, which Wilde adored and reviewed.
text: The book calls the Lyceum the most fashionable of theatres. Irving took over its management in 1878 with Ellen Terry as leading lady, a partnership that lasted until 1902. Irving's Mathias in The Bells, repeated more than eight hundred times, was the sensation of the age. The book reproduces Irving and Terry in Much Ado About Nothing (11 October 1882).

Wilde was devoted to both, and the book quotes at length his 1885 review of their Hamlet, praising Irving's 'personality and perfection' and Terry's Ophelia. Bram Stoker, Irving's business manager and later author of Dracula, had married Florence Balcombe, the Dublin girl Wilde had courted.
events: Irving takes over the Lyceum with Ellen Terry.
Irving and Terry in Much Ado About Nothing.

images.caption: Irving's Faust at the Lyceum, The Graphic, 1886
images.author: The Graphic

places.name: Gaiety Theatre
places.address: Strand, at Wellington Street (old theatre demolished 1903)
places.summary: Where Sarah Bernhardt played with the Comédie-Française in 1879, and later George Edwardes's house of musical comedy and 'Gaiety Girls'.
text: In June 1879 the Comédie-Française brought its stars to the Gaiety. Wilde met Sarah Bernhardt's boat at Folkestone with an armful of lilies and wrote her a sonnet. The book records his remark that the three women he most admired were Queen Victoria, Sarah Bernhardt and Lillie Langtry.

Under George Edwardes in the 1890s the Gaiety invented musical comedy, with A Gaiety Girl, The Shop Girl and The Circus Girl. The book quotes W. S. Gilbert, under cross-examination by Edward Carson, calling The Circus Girl 'bad', a fine piece of Wilde-trial foreshadowing.
events: Sarah Bernhardt's London debut season with the Comédie-Française.
The Shop Girl opens: musical comedy arrives.

places.name: Theatre Royal, Drury Lane
places.summary: Augustus Harris's home of spectacular melodrama and the Christmas pantomime, where Dan Leno reigned.
text: Augustus Harris ran Drury Lane from 1879, staging lavish melodramas and pantomimes and recruiting music-hall stars to them from 1880, which helped make the halls respectable, as the book explains. Wagner's Flying Dutchman had its London premiere here in 1870, in Italian.

The book quotes the Sunday Times correspondent who thought even the boxes at Covent Garden and Drury Lane could not match the noise of a Marylebone penny gaff. It also records Gilbert's quip that the Drury Lane pantomime with 'the great Dan Leno' was only a short season but went on 'a long time in the evening'.
events: Drury Lane brings music-hall stars into its pantomime.

images.caption: Dan Leno as the Baroness in Cinderella
images.author: Alfred Ellis

places.name: Royal Opera House, Covent Garden
places.summary: The Royal Italian Opera became the Royal Opera in 1892 under Augustus Harris; Patti, Melba and the de Reszkes sang here.
text: The book traces London opera's swing from the dogma that good opera was Italian to the Wagner craze. Lohengrin was given here in 1875 and Tannhäuser in 1876, both in Italian. Adelina Patti made her debut here in 1861 and, the book notes, earned two hundred guineas a performance. Jean de Reszke conquered London as Radamès in Aida in 1887.

Augustus Harris took over in 1888 and gave London polyglot seasons in French, German and Italian. The house was renamed the Royal Opera in 1892. At the 1879 Christmas pantomime, music-hall stars Herbert Campbell and the Great MacDermott appeared on its stage.
events: Jean de Reszke's triumph in Aida.
Augustus Harris takes over Covent Garden.

images.caption: Adelina Patti and Giovanni Mario in Faust, 1864
images.author: Caldesi & Co.

places.name: Her Majesty's Theatre
places.summary: Where London first heard Wagner's complete Ring cycle in German, in 1882.
text: Angelo Neumann's touring company brought the whole Ring here in May 1882, the first time London heard Wagner in German. The book quotes the Standard's disgust at its 'childish dragons, bears, alligators' and Punch's 'Wagnerian Waggeries' alongside the Times's praise. When his son was born in 1885, Wilde joked that the baby's voice was 'essentially Wagnerian'.
The old theatre was demolished in 1892. Herbert Beerbohm Tree, who had staged A Woman of No Importance across the road, built the present house in 1897.
events: First complete Ring in German in London.
Tree opens the new Her Majesty's.

places.name: Garrick Theatre
places.summary: Built for John Hare and opened in 1889 with Pinero's The Profligate, a play about the sexual double standard.
text: The book describes how John Hare moved here from the St James's when the theatre was built for him 'near the foot of Charing Cross Road'. It opened in April 1889 with Pinero's The Profligate, which asked whether a husband should be as chaste as he expected his wife to be.
The book counts the play as the start of Pinero's career as a serious social dramatist, a step toward the 'woman with a past' plays of the 1890s that Wilde would rework into comedy.

images.caption: The Garrick Theatre, Charing Cross Road
images.author: Jim Osley

places.name: Novelty Theatre: A Doll's House
places.address: Great Queen Street (later the Kingsway Theatre; demolished)
places.summary: Where William Archer's translation of A Doll's House opened in June 1889 and brought Ibsen to the English stage.
text: The book credits William Archer, backed by Shaw, Eleanor Marx, Edward Aveling and May Morris, with winning London over to Ibsen. Archer's translation of A Doll's House opened at this small theatre in 1889, with Janet Achurch as Nora, and 'at last secured for Ibsen a prominent place on the English stage'.

The book contrasts this with Henry Arthur Jones's 1884 travesty, The Breaking of a Butterfly, and with Clement Scott's protest that the playhouse 'is not a charnel house'. Wilde admired Ibsen and borrowed from his drama of hidden pasts.

images.caption: The Novelty Theatre, Great Queen Street, 1882
images.author: Unknown author

places.name: Vaudeville Theatre
places.summary: Ibsen's Rosmersholm was staged here in 1891.
text: The book reproduces the Illustrated Sporting and Dramatic News's scenes from Rosmersholm here in 1891. By then, it says, Ibsen was established on the London stage despite the critics.

1891 was the year of the 'Ibsen controversy': Ghosts at the Independent Theatre, Hedda Gabler with Elizabeth Robins, and Rosmersholm here. Wilde went to Hedda Gabler and wrote to Robins that he felt 'pity and terror'.

images.caption: Programme: That Doctor Cupid at the Vaudeville Theatre, c. 1887 (British Library)
images.author: Southwold1966

places.name: Sadler's Wells
places.summary: London's oldest theatre went from skating rink to variety house, with Chaplin's father on the bill in 1891 and an early cinema show.
text: The book follows the Wells through the period. It became a roller-skating rink in 1876, then hosted the magician Professor Pepper, circus troupes and illegal prize fights. Mrs Bateman, who had just sold the Lyceum to Irving, took it over in 1878. In 1891 the bill included one Charles Chaplin, whose son and namesake was two years old.

In the 1890s the manager George Belmont, 'the Aristocrat of Alliteration', billed Marie Lloyd as 'the Divine Droll' and introduced R. W. Paul's Theatrograph to his audiences. Pinero's Trelawny of the 'Wells' (1898) remembered its older days.
events: Sadler's Wells becomes a skating rink.
Charles Chaplin senior on the bill.

places.name: Prince of Wales's Theatre (Tottenham Street)
places.summary: The Bancrofts' little theatre of 'cup and saucer' realism, where Burnand's satire of the aesthetes, The Colonel, played in 1881.
text: The Bancrofts made their name here from 1865 with T. W. Robertson's 'cup and saucer' domestic comedies, which the book says seemed true to life but 'wooden'. Ellen Terry acted with them on her return to the stage in 1875. (The book places the theatre on Coventry Street. That was a later Prince of Wales's, built in 1884.)

F. C. Burnand's The Colonel, a satire of 'the foolish aesthetic people', opened here in February 1881, two months before Patience. The book argues it may have pushed Gilbert to turn his clergyman hero into the poet Bunthorne. It was the first play Queen Victoria saw after twenty years of mourning, in a command performance at Abergeldie.
events: The Colonel opens, satirising the aesthetes.

images.caption: Burnand's The Colonel in an 1887 revival
images.author: London Stereoscopic Co.

places.name: Prince of Wales's Theatre (Coventry Street)
places.summary: Where Edwardes's A Gaiety Girl launched the musical-comedy craze.
text: The book reproduces Dudley Hardy's poster for A Gaiety Girl, the show that founded the new genre of musical comedy, and notes that 'the showgirl became the stuff of comedy'. (The book dates the poster to 1895. The show opened here in October 1893.)
Built in 1884 as the Prince's Theatre and renamed in 1886, the theatre stood on the corner of the Leicester Square entertainment district.

images.caption: Dudley Hardy, poster for A Gaiety Girl
images.author: Dudley Hardy

places.name: Princess's Theatre
places.summary: Oxford Street's melodrama house, where How London Lives played to packed houses.
text: The book reproduces the sheet-music cover for 'How London Lives', a song from the melodrama of that name at the Princess's. Sheet music from publishers like Francis, Day & Hunter of Charing Cross Road carried theatre and music-hall hits into every parlour with a piano.
Melodrama of the Princess's kind, with its sensation scenes and virtue rewarded, was the theatre Wilde mocked and then turned to his own uses in his society plays.

places.name: Alhambra Theatre of Varieties
places.summary: Moorish palace of variety and ballet, where Léotard flew and R. W. Paul's film of the 1896 Derby was shown the next night.
text: The acrobat Léotard played the Alhambra in the 1860s, inspiring 'The Daring Young Man on the Flying Trapeze', as the book notes. By the 1890s it was one of the two great variety theatres on Leicester Square, with lavish ballets and a promenade where the audience strolled, drank and looked for company.
In June 1896 the Alhambra commissioned R. W. Paul to film the Derby, won by the Prince of Wales's horse Persimmon. The film was shown here the following evening, one of the first newsreels.
events: Paul's film of the Derby shown the evening after the race.

images.caption: Leicester Square with the Alhambra, Illustrated London News, 1874
images.author: Frank Watkins (illustrator)

places.name: Empire Theatre of Varieties
places.summary: Its promenade behind the dress circle was, the book says, one of the best places in London to pick someone up.
text: The book quotes Harper's Monthly (1891) on the Empire: stained glass, electric lamps, smoking everywhere, men in evening dress, an audience paying little attention to the dazzling ballets, and women 'pretty obvious members of a class' that 'it would be neither desirable nor possible to exclude'. The promenade, it says, 'provided one of the best chances for a pickup in London'.

In 1894 the purity campaigner Laura Ormiston Chant persuaded the LCC to screen the promenade off, and young men, Winston Churchill among them, tore the screens down. Historians of queer London note that men cruised the promenade too.
events: The Empire promenade controversy; screens torn down.

images.caption: Empire Theatre, Round the World, 1885
