images.author: Unknown, edited by Émile Lévy, Paris. Uploaded, stiched and restored by JLPC

places.name: Canterbury Music Hall
places.summary: Charles Morton's Canterbury Arms of 1852, the first building designed as a music hall.
text: The book traces the music hall from pleasure gardens, glee clubs and tavern sing-songs to Charles Morton's Canterbury of 1852, the first purpose-built hall. By 1860 there were more than 250 halls in London.

It describes how the 1878 licensing law closed shabby halls, how stars like the Great MacDermott, George Leybourne ('Champagne Charlie') and Marie Lloyd drew the middle classes, and how chains of Empires and Hippodromes followed in the 1890s. It quotes T. S. Eliot's tribute to Lloyd, who in his view gave the working class 'the artistic expression and dignity of their own lives'.

places.name: Royal Victoria Coffee Music Hall (the Old Vic)
places.summary: Emma Cons's temperance music hall of 1880, offering entertainment without the drink.
text: The reformer Emma Cons took over the rowdy Royal Victoria Theatre in 1880 and reopened it as the Royal Victoria Coffee Music Hall: variety, ballad concerts and lectures, with coffee instead of gin. The book reproduces The Graphic's 1882 drawing of its Christmas pantomime audience, mostly children, crying 'Sit Down in Front'.
It belongs to the book's story of temperance and rational recreation, and the beginnings of the Old Vic and of Morley College.
events: Emma Cons opens the Coffee Music Hall.

places.name: Queen's Hall
places.summary: Concert hall where Henry Wood began the Promenade Concerts in 1895.
text: The book notes that the Queen's Hall Promenade Concerts, begun by Henry Wood in 1895, gave orchestral music a new public, continuing a tradition of Crystal Palace concerts that went back to 1855.

Wood's cheap standing tickets suited the improving tastes of the new clerks and shop-workers who, the book says, flooded the West End in the evenings. The hall was destroyed in the Blitz and the Proms moved to the Albert Hall.

images.caption: The opening of the Queen's Hall, 1893
images.author: Raymond Potter

places.name: Royal Albert Hall
places.summary: The Prince Consort's memorial hall of arts and sciences (1871), centre of London's choral and concert life.
text: The book reproduces a view of Fowke and Scott's great oval, completed in 1871, and calls it the foremost centre of London's musical life. It was the stage for the enormous choral and oratorio performances whose popularity Shaw mocked.
The book's account of the choral movement, with tonic sol-fa teaching and choirs and competitions, belongs here. So does its picture of Parry and Stanford at the 'dull center' of the oratorio.

images.caption: The opening of the Royal Albert Hall by Queen Victoria, The Graphic, 1871
images.author: Unknown author

places.name: Egyptian Hall
places.summary: 'England's Home of Mystery', where Maskelyne and Cooke performed magic from the 1870s and London saw early films in 1896.
text: Behind its pharaonic facade, John Nevil Maskelyne and George Cooke staged illusions here from the 1870s, including Maskelyne's 'Box Trick'. The book retells Dr Lynn's 'Palingenesia', in which a volunteer was apparently cut to pieces and restored.

Maskelyne also debunked spiritualist mediums and appeared as an expert witness against the American medium Henry Slade in 1876. The book reproduces a poster for 'Animated Photographs' and dates London's first cinematograph shows here to 1896.
events: Animated photographs shown at the Egyptian Hall.

images.caption: The Egyptian Hall, Piccadilly (Shepherd, Metropolitan Improvements, 1828)
images.author: Thomas Hosmer Shepherd

places.name: Royal Polytechnic Institution
places.summary: Home of 'Pepper's Ghost' and scientific entertainments, refounded in 1882 as a Polytechnic for working men.
text: The book's Professor Pepper, 'late of the Royal Polytechnic', made his name here with the stage illusion of 'Pepper's Ghost' and magic-lantern shows that mixed science with spectacle.

In 1882 Quintin Hogg bought the building for his Young Men's Christian Institute, which became the Regent Street Polytechnic, a model of the self-improvement the book describes among the working and lower-middle classes.

images.caption: Pepper's Ghost, as staged at the Polytechnic
images.author: Bertrand (no first name given)

places.name: Astley's Amphitheatre
places.summary: London's only permanent circus building, run from 1871 by 'Lord' George Sanger.
text: Philip Astley invented the modern circus here in the 1760s, with equestrian feats in a ring. The book follows George Sanger, son of a travelling peep-show man, who took over in 1871 and staged spectacles such as 'Lady Godiva'. When Astley's was demolished in 1893, London lost its only permanent circus.
The book tells how Queen Victoria, having summoned Sanger to Windsor in 1899, teased him about his self-awarded title: 'Lord George Sanger, I believe?'

images.caption: Astley's Amphitheatre
images.author: Engraving by Charles John Smith (1808–38) after William Capon.

places.name: A Marylebone penny gaff
places.summary: The poor man's theatre: a shop with its window knocked out, a stage the size of a railway carriage, and Dick Whittington for a penny.
text: The book reprints a Sunday Times correspondent's visit to a penny gaff in the Marylebone streets 'ablaze with naphtha', among butchers' stalls and costers' cries. The 'gorgeous ballet pantomime' advertised outside turned out to be a clown, a pantaloon, a harlequin and a policeman on a stage 'about the size of an ordinary third-class railway carriage'.

Nothing, the writer said, matched the laughter of the 'leather-lunged ragged little brothers and sisters' in the audience. The exact address is not given. The marker stands for the street-market district north of the Marylebone Road.

places.name: Liberty & Co.
places.address: East India House, 218a Regent Street (rebuilt; Tudor building of 1924 behind)
places.summary: Arthur Lasenby Liberty's 'art warehouse' of 1875, where the 'vegetable fashion' of Aestheticism began.
text: The book traces the 'sentimental passion for a vegetable fashion' to the small shop Liberty opened on Regent Street in 1875, selling Oriental silks and soft-coloured fabrics: 'Persian pink, Venetian red, terracotta, ocher-yellow, sapphire and peacock blue'. Its customers included Burne-Jones, Whistler, Norman Shaw and Godwin, and the costume designers of Patience.

Liberty opened in Paris in 1884, and the style it sold became international as Art Nouveau, or Stile Liberty in Italy. The book makes it the starting point of a style that ran from Beardsley to Tiffany and Gaudí.

images.caption: Liberty's Tudor building (1924), Great Marlborough Street
images.author: John Winfield

places.name: Morris & Co. showroom
places.summary: The West End shop of 'The Firm', selling William Morris's wallpapers, chintzes, furniture and glass.
text: The book reproduces the shopfront of Morris & Co. at 449 Oxford Street, the outlet for 'The Firm' from 1877. Here Morris's 'Acanthus' damask, 'Saville' chairs and stained glass were sold to the fashionable and wealthy, which troubled their socialist designer.

The book sets out the dilemma. Morris wanted beauty in every home, but hand-made goods were luxuries, and he eventually allowed cheaper machine-made versions, which 'sold well'. On his Social Democratic Federation card he described himself as 'Designer'.
events: Morris & Co. opens at 449 Oxford Street.

places.name: Kelmscott House and the Kelmscott Press
places.summary: William Morris's riverside home, meeting place of the Hammersmith Socialist League and, from 1891, his private press.
text: Morris lived here from 1878 until his death in 1896. The coach house hosted the Hammersmith branch of the Socialist League, which the book illustrates, and lectures by Shaw, Kropotkin and others. Nearby on the Upper Mall he founded the Kelmscott Press in 1891. Morris designed his own Golden, Troy and Chaucer types and printed by hand on handmade paper.

The book reproduces the press's March 1894 prospectus and the Labour Prophet's 1896 obituary of Morris. It sets Morris's populist vision against the elitism of Wilde and Whistler and suggests that 'It should have been a nice balance'.

images.caption: James Richard Marquis, Hammersmith from Barnes
images.author: James Richard Marquis

places.name: 49 Prince's Gate: the Peacock Room
places.address: 49 Prince's Gate, Kensington (room now in the Freer Gallery, Washington)
places.summary: Frederick Leyland's dining room, painted by Whistler as 'Harmony in Blue and Gold', the most talked-about interior of the age.
text: The book quotes The Times of 15 February 1877 on Whistler's decoration of the shipowner Frederick Leyland's dining room: ornament 'entirely derived from the beautiful plumage of the peacock', 'completely Japanesque'. Whistler painted over Thomas Jeckyll's leather-hung room without permission and fell out bitterly with Leyland over the fee.

The room is the book's example of the Japanese craze, from fans and 'Tokio Tooth Powder' to Godwin's furniture and Worcester's satirical Aesthetic teapot. It was sold in 1904 and now stands in the Freer Gallery in Washington.
events: The Times praises the Peacock Room.

images.caption: Whistler, Harmony in Blue and Gold: The Peacock Room
images.author: James McNeill Whistler

places.name: The Japanese Native Village, Knightsbridge
places.summary: A walk-through 'village' of Japanese craftsmen (1885–87), credited with inspiring The Mikado.
text: From January 1885 Londoners paid to watch Japanese artisans, tea-house girls and performers in a reconstructed village in Knightsbridge. The Savoy's Mikado programmes, reproduced in the book, credit the 'Native Inhabitants of the Japanese Village, Knightsbridge' for coaching the company in Japanese manners.
The village sums up what the book calls the 'Japanesque' rage: Japan as a consumer fantasy, in Godwin's furniture, Wedgwood's 'Sparrow and Bamboo' service and Beardsley's prints.

images.caption: Afternoon tea at the Japanese Village, Knightsbridge, 1886
images.author: British Library Newspapers (March 13, 1886), London, England.

places.name: Leighton House
places.summary: Frederic Leighton's studio-palace with its tiled Arab Hall, a showpiece of artistic Kensington.
text: Lord Leighton, President of the Royal Academy, built this house from 1864 and added the domed Arab Hall, lined with Iznik and Damascus tiles, in 1877–81. The 'Holland Park circle' of studio-houses around it was the Academic counterpart to Chelsea's Bohemia.

The book's chapter on 'Lilies and Sunflowers' describes how art took over the domestic interior. Leighton House was its most opulent example, and fashionable London visited the studio on 'Show Sunday' before the Academy opened.

places.name: South Kensington Museum
places.address: Cromwell Road (now the Victoria and Albert Museum)
places.summary: The museum of decorative arts, with Morris's Green Dining Room, which supplied many of the book's pictures.
text: Founded after the Great Exhibition to raise the standard of British design, the museum commissioned Morris's firm to decorate its Green Dining Room in 1866–68. The book's credit lines show its debt to the collection, now the V&A: Morris interiors, Beardsley's Morte d'Arthur binding, Paul Martin's street photographs and Hollyer's portraits.
The building tells the story the book tells about the 'Arts and Crafts' faith that beautiful surroundings make better people, and that design could be taught.

places.name: Albert Memorial
places.summary: Gilbert Scott's 175-foot Gothic reliquary for the Prince Consort, completed in 1872–76.
text: The book reproduces the memorial and describes it as 'a gigantic medieval reliquary'. The gilded prince sits under a pinnacled canopy with groups representing Engineering, Agriculture, Manufactures and Commerce, and the four continents at the corners.
It is the book's example of Ruskin's influence on architecture: the Gothic as the only virtuous style, at a scale only an empire could afford.

places.name: Collingham Gardens
places.summary: Ernest George and Peto's picturesque gabled houses, which the book holds up as typical 'Queen Anne'/Arts and Crafts design.
text: The book illustrates Collingham Gardens, built in the mid-1880s, as a typical Arts and Crafts development. Its Flemish gables, terracotta and varied fronts were a reaction against the uniform stucco terraces of Kensington.

This was the 'Queen Anne' style the book explains as Gothic bones with Classical flesh (Mark Girouard's phrase). It had nothing to do with Queen Anne, and the Wildes' house in Tite Street was built in the same manner.

places.name: Bedford Park
places.summary: The first garden suburb, Norman Shaw's red-brick 'Queen Anne' village for artistic commuters, where the Yeats family lived.
text: Begun in 1875–77 by Jonathan Carr with houses largely by Norman Shaw, Bedford Park was built for aesthetic middle-class families. It had its own church, inn, art school and stores, and was a short train ride from town. The book calls Shaw 'probably London's busiest architect' and the acknowledged master of the 'Queen Anne' style.
W. B. Yeats grew up here. Bedford Park also anticipates the garden cities of Ebenezer Howard, with which the book ends.

images.caption: Part of the Bedford Park estate, colour lithograph, 1882
images.author: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/obf_images/48/05/bd7c60899ffc2c410c46337eace1.jpg Gallery: http

places.name: Carlyle's House
places.summary: Home of the Victorian sage Thomas Carlyle until his death in 1881. His writing desk ended up in Wilde's study.
text: Thomas Carlyle, the 'Sage of Chelsea', lived here from 1834 until 1881. The book lists, among the few furnishings of Wilde's study at Tite Street, 'a large writing-desk which had once belonged to Thomas Carlyle'. Most of Wilde's serious work was done at it.
The house opened as a museum in 1895, the year Wilde's desk and everything else he owned were sold off.
events: Carlyle's House opens as a museum.

places.name: 16 Cheyne Walk: Rossetti and Swinburne
places.summary: Dante Gabriel Rossetti's house of curios and wombats, centre of the Chelsea Bohemia that Wilde set out to conquer.
text: The book quotes Beerbohm: 'Swinburne, Morris, Rossetti, Whistler, Burne-Jones' formed the 'little community' of Chelsea where the new art was born, quietly showing one another their poems and pictures. Rossetti lived here from 1862 until his death in 1882, with a menagerie that included a wombat. Swinburne shared the house for a time.

Beerbohm describes Wilde's Poems as a 'decoy to the shy artificers of Chelsea'. The book reproduces Rossetti's self-portrait and his painting of Jane Morris, the face that 'made red hair and prominent upper lips fashionable'.

images.caption: Henry Treffry Dunn, Rossetti's studio at Cheyne Walk, 1881
images.author: Henry Treffry Dunn

places.name: Whistler's Thames: 96 Cheyne Walk
places.summary: Whistler's home in the years he painted the Nocturnes of the river at Battersea and Chelsea.
text: From windows on this stretch of the river Whistler watched the evening mist turn chimneys into campanili and warehouses into palaces, as his 'Ten O'Clock' put it. The book quotes the passage and calls it the lesson in how 'to appreciate the beauty of the city'. The Nocturnes he painted here, including the Falling Rocket the book reproduces, are the source of Wilde's Thames poems.

Wilde turned the idea into a paradox: 'At present, people see fogs, not because there are fogs, but because poets and painters have taught them the mysterious loveliness of such effects.' The book quotes the line from 'The Decay of Lying'.

images.caption: Whistler, Nocturne: Blue and Gold – Old Battersea Bridge
images.author: James McNeill Whistler

places.name: Chelsea Embankment
places.address: Chelsea Embankment, between Chelsea Bridge and Battersea Bridge
places.summary: Bazalgette's new riverside road (1874), which cut Chelsea off from its old foreshore and gave Tite Street its esplanade.
text: The book notes that Tite Street lay near the 'lovely esplanade' of the Chelsea Embankment, completed just before the Wildes moved in. The embankment carried Bazalgette's low-level sewer and a new road along the river, and sealed off the muddy foreshore and boatyards of old Chelsea that Whistler and Turner had painted.
The mansion blocks and studio houses that rose behind it replaced the riverside slums. The book points out that Tite Street still faced slums across the way.

images.caption: Frederick Brown, An Impromptu Dance: a scene on the Chelsea Embankment, 1883
images.author: Frederick Brown

places.name: Royal Hospital, Chelsea
places.summary: Wren's home for army pensioners, whose gardens bordered Wilde's Tite Street.
text: The book places Tite Street 'just west of the Chelsea Hospital Gardens', where the Chelsea Flower Show is now held every May. Wren's red-brick hospital for veteran soldiers, with its scarlet-coated pensioners, was one of Chelsea's institutions.
The contrast is the one the book keeps returning to: imperial London, with its veterans and its monuments, a few hundred yards from an aesthete's study.

places.name: Frederick Hollyer's studio
places.summary: The photographer whose portraits of Morris, Ruskin, Burne-Jones and Beardsley illustrate the book.
text: Frederick Hollyer photographed the artists of the Aesthetic and Arts and Crafts movements at his Kensington studio, where his 'Hollyer Mondays' were open days for sitters. The book reproduces his portraits of William Morris (1884), John Ruskin, Burne-Jones and Aubrey Beardsley.
These are the images through which we still picture the movement's heroes, and they were made with the same care for craft the sitters preached.

images.caption: Frederick Hollyer, Burne-Jones and William Morris, 1874
images.author: Frederick Hollyer

places.name: New Gallery: the Arts and Crafts Exhibition
places.summary: Where the Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society, which gave the movement its name, held its shows from 1888.
text: Founded by former Grosvenor Gallery managers in 1888, the New Gallery hosted the Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society's first exhibitions, with lectures by Morris, Crane and Lethaby. Wilde reviewed the 1888 lectures, by Morris, Crane, Emery Walker and Cobden-Sanderson, for the Pall Mall Gazette.
The book quotes Lethaby's 1896 lecture from this series ('London is as structureless as one of its own fogs') as a statement of civic Aestheticism, about better lamp-posts and cleaner streets.

places.name: Central School of Arts and Crafts
places.summary: The LCC's school of design, founded in 1896 with W. R. Lethaby as principal.
text: The book introduces 'the architect William Richard Lethaby, who founded London's Central School of Arts and Crafts'. The London County Council opened it in 1896 to train craftsmen in workshops rather than in academic drawing.
It is the institutional end of the Arts and Crafts faith the book describes, that design reform could reach everyone. Its later move to Southampton Row made it a cradle of modern design.
events: Central School of Arts and Crafts opens.

images.caption: The Central School of Arts and Crafts, Southampton Row
images.author: Spudgun67

places.name: National Gallery of British Art (the Tate)
places.summary: Opened in July 1897 on the site of Millbank Penitentiary, just after Wilde left England. Its collection supplies many of the book's paintings.
text: Henry Tate's gallery of British art opened on 21 July 1897, on the site of the demolished Millbank prison. The book draws on it for Burne-Jones's King Cophetua, Waterhouse's Lady of Shalott, Millais's Ophelia, Charles Keene's sketches and its jacket picture, Atkinson Grimshaw's view of Heath Street by night.
There is an irony in the site. The new temple of art rose where London's largest prison had stood, two months after Wilde walked out of Pentonville.
events: The Tate Gallery opens at Millbank.

images.caption: John Varley, The Thames near the Penitentiary, Millbank
images.author: John Varley

places.name: Heath Street, Hampstead, by night
places.summary: The village street in Atkinson Grimshaw's nocturne on the book's jacket.
text: The book's front jacket reproduces Atkinson Grimshaw's moonlit painting of Heath Street, with gaslight on wet cobbles and figures half-dissolved in the gloom. Grimshaw was Whistler's commercial rival in painting the poetry of the night city. Whistler is said to have admitted that he thought he had invented the nocturne until he saw 'Grimmy's' moonlights.

The painting fits the book's argument that Wilde's generation discovered romance in 'bricks and mortar', in what Holbrook Jackson called streets, theatres and taverns rather than wild nature. (The book's jacket note dates the painting to 1888 and credits the Tate Gallery.)

images.caption: John Atkinson Grimshaw, View of Heath Street by Night
images.author: John Atkinson Grimshaw

places.name: St Paul's Cathedral: 'Impression du Matin'
places.summary: The dome that 'loomed like a bubble o'er the town' in Wilde's Whistlerian Thames poem, and the setting of the 1897 Jubilee service.
text: The book prints Wilde's 'Impression du Matin' from Poems (1881) in full. A Thames 'nocturne of blue and gold' turns to grey, the yellow fog creeps down the bridges, 'St. Paul's / Loomed like a bubble o'er the town', and the poem ends on a woman loitering under the gas lamps 'with lips of flame and heart of stone'.

The book reads the poem as both 'precious in its romanticism and precise in its realism'. In June 1897 Victoria's Diamond Jubilee thanksgiving was held on the cathedral steps because the old queen could not climb them.
events: Diamond Jubilee service at St Paul's.

images.caption: John Gendall, St Paul's Cathedral from the Thames
images.author: John Gendall

places.name: The Pines, Putney: Swinburne
places.summary: Where the poet Swinburne, rescued from drink by Theodore Watts-Dunton, lived in suburban quiet from 1879.
text: The book describes the young Swinburne 'quivering with passion' as he recited 'Dolores' to kneeling Pre-Raphaelite ladies, and notes that he 'reveled in vices rather than virtues' and lost the laureateship to Alfred Austin. In 1879, the year Wilde reached London, Watts-Dunton removed him to this semi-detached villa in Putney, where he lived soberly for thirty years.
The move from Chelsea to Putney shows one Aesthetic hero retiring to the suburbs just as Wilde arrived to carry the cause into society.

places.name: Fleet Street
places.address: Fleet Street, from Temple Bar to Ludgate Circus
places.summary: The street of newspapers, where Willie Wilde wrote for the Daily Telegraph and Punch mocked his brother.
text: 'Virtually all of London's newspapers', the book says, had their printing plants and offices on Fleet Street, from the respectable Times to what after 1895 was called the 'yellow press'. Paper boys chanting headlines darted through the traffic. Punch, whose cartoons of 'O.W.' as a sunflower-worshipping aesthete the book reproduces, had its offices at 85 Fleet Street.

Oscar's brother Willie wrote leaders for the Daily Telegraph, whose star George Augustus Sala produced two articles a day for a quarter of a century and helped found the Savage Club. The book quotes Holbrook Jackson: poets now 'invoked the Muses in Fleet Street and the Strand'.

images.caption: Fleet Street, c. 1890, photographed by James Valentine
images.author: Unknown

places.name: Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese: the Rhymers' Club
places.summary: The old chop-house where Yeats, Dowson, Johnson and the Rhymers read their poems to one another from 1890.
text: The book describes the Rhymers' Club as an attempt to revive the eighteenth-century literary tavern, with a dozen poets reading in alphabetical order, 'typically beginning with Ernest Dowson and ending with W. B. Yeats'. They met in an upstairs room of this Fleet Street tavern, Johnson's old haunt. (The book puts the Cheese 'in the Strand'.)

Wilde, the book says, came only when the club met in a private house. The Rhymers published two anthologies (1892, 1894) and supplied the Bodley Head and the Savoy with its 'tragic generation' of poets.
events: First Book of the Rhymers' Club.

images.caption: The dining room of Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese, with its high-backed settles, from The Book of the Cheese
images.author: Internet Archive Book Images

places.name: Pall Mall Gazette: Stead's 'Maiden Tribute'
places.summary: W. T. Stead's evening paper, which published Wilde's reviews and, in July 1885, the sensational 'Maiden Tribute of Modern Babylon'.
text: Under W. T. Stead the Pall Mall Gazette pioneered the 'new journalism' of interviews and exposés. From 1885 to 1890 Wilde reviewed books for it, including Whistler's 'Ten O'Clock'. The book shows Stead setting Annie Besant to review Madame Blavatsky's Secret Doctrine because she was 'quite mad enough on the subject'.

On 6 July 1885 the paper began 'The Maiden Tribute of Modern Babylon', under the headline 'A Child of Thirteen Bought for £5'. The book reprints the story of 'Lily' (Eliza Armstrong) and condemns it as a 'pseudo-event', set up with Bramwell Booth of the Salvation Army. Stead was sentenced to three months for abduction (the book says two). The uproar pushed through the Criminal Law Amendment Act of 1885, which raised the age of consent to sixteen and carried Labouchère's clause against 'gross indecency' between men.
events: Criminal Law Amendment Act passed, with the Labouchère amendment.

images.caption: Stead in convict dress after the Armstrong case
images.author: Unknown author

places.name: The Bodley Head: The Yellow Book
places.summary: Elkin Mathews and John Lane's shop and imprint: Wilde's Salome and The Sphinx, Beardsley and The Yellow Book.
text: The book counts the Bodley Head among the small, daring publishers who 'prided themselves in serving the Muses rather than Mammon'. It published Wilde's Lady Windermere's Fan, Salome (1894, illustrated by Beardsley), The Sphinx (designed by Charles Ricketts) and The Yellow Book, whose April 1894 first number, with Beardsley's black-and-yellow cover, the book reproduces.

Wilde never wrote for The Yellow Book. But when he was arrested on 5 April 1895, reportedly carrying a yellow-backed French novel, the newspapers said 'Arrest of Oscar Wilde, Yellow Book under his arm'. A crowd broke the windows here. Lane withdrew Wilde's books and dismissed Beardsley from The Yellow Book.
events: First number of The Yellow Book.
Windows smashed; Beardsley dropped from The Yellow Book.

images.caption: The Yellow Book, vol. 1, April 1894, cover by Beardsley
images.author: Aubrey Beardsley

places.name: Leonard Smithers, Royal Arcade
places.summary: The 'most learned erotomaniac in Europe': publisher of The Savoy, Beardsley, Dowson and, in 1898, The Ballad of Reading Gaol.
text: The book quotes Wilde's description of Smithers as 'the most learned erotomaniac in Europe'. Smithers published the decadents nobody else would touch: Arthur Symons's London Nights, Dowson, Beardsley's late drawings and The Savoy (1896). After his release Wilde had no other publisher, and Smithers brought out The Ballad of Reading Gaol in 1898.
The book also reports that his shop sold 'artistically posed' photographs of young girls. And it notes that Beardsley, dying in 1898, begged Smithers to destroy his erotic drawings; Smithers did not.
events: The Ballad of Reading Gaol published.

images.caption: The Royal Arcade, Old Bond Street
images.author: Tony Hisgett from Birmingham, UK

places.name: Charing Cross Road: bookshops
places.summary: The new street of bookshops, where a clerk might serve fourteen years before he counted as qualified.
text: Cut through the slums of St Giles and opened in 1887, Charing Cross Road quickly filled with booksellers. The book says 'most London bookstores' were here, 'thriving, serious businesses'. Its customers wanted everything from penny dreadfuls and shilling shockers to Marie Corelli, the Queen's favourite novelist.
Music publishers came too. The book reproduces sheet music from Francis, Day & Hunter at 142 Charing Cross Road, whose songs carried the hits of the halls into parlours across the country.

places.name: Ludgate Circus
places.address: Ludgate Circus, at the foot of Fleet Street
places.summary: Where Paul Martin photographed a magazine seller, and the river of news met the traffic of the City.
text: The book reproduces Paul Martin's candid photograph of a magazine seller at Ludgate Circus. Reading journals, novels and pamphlets, it says, had become a sign of middle-class respectability. Nearby it shows a newsstand on Newgate Street.
Martin's hand-held 'detective' camera allowed him to catch Londoners unposed. His pictures of the Thames Embankment, Victoria Park and Battersea fair are among the book's most vivid.

images.caption: Gustave Doré, Ludgate Hill: A Block in the Street, 1872
images.author: Gustave Doré (1832-1883)

places.name: Chapman & Hall: The Fortnightly Review
places.summary: Where 'The Soul of Man under Socialism' appeared in February 1891.
text: The Fortnightly Review, published by Chapman & Hall, serialised Trollope's novels, as the book notes, and in February 1891 printed Wilde's 'The Soul of Man under Socialism'. The book quotes it often: 'Disobedience... is man's original virtue', 'to recommend thrift to the poor is both grotesque and insulting', and 'The new Individualism is the new Hellenism.'
The book notes that even skeptical socialists took the essay seriously. It was translated widely, especially in Russia and central Europe.
events: 'The Soul of Man under Socialism' published.

places.name: David Nutt: The Happy Prince
places.summary: The scholarly publisher who brought out The Happy Prince and Other Tales in May 1888.
text: Nutt, a publisher of folklore and scholarship, issued Wilde's fairy tales with illustrations by Walter Crane and Jacomb Hood. Walter Pater, the book's prophet of 'art for art's sake', wrote to praise them.

The book's discussion of illustrators names Crane, Kate Greenaway and Randolph Caldecott. This little book brought Wilde and Crane together, and its sad, selfless heroes sit oddly with the dandy's public image.
events: The Happy Prince and Other Tales published.

images.caption: Walter Crane, plate from The Happy Prince and Other Tales, 1888
images.author: Crane, Walter, 1845-1915

places.name: British Museum Reading Room
places.summary: The domed reading room where Marx had worked, and where Amy Levy, Eleanor Marx, Shaw and a generation of 'New Women' wrote.
text: The book notes that working people sought the quiet of library reading rooms to escape overcrowded homes. The British Museum's Reading Room was the summit of that world, and a meeting place for the socialists, Fabians and women writers the book describes: Eleanor Marx, Shaw, Beatrice Potter, Amy Levy.
Women's presence among the readers was itself news in the 1880s, and part of the 'New Woman' the book lists among the decade's novelties, alongside the New Realism and the New Hedonism.

images.caption: The Reading Room of the British Museum
images.author: Robert-brook

places.name: Inner Temple: Gandhi in London
places.summary: Where Mohandas K. Gandhi, the young law student the book mentions, read for the bar from 1888 to 1891.
text: The book notes that among Annie Besant's admirers was 'a twenty-one-year-old Indian law student living in London at the time'. Gandhi came to London in 1888, joined the Inner Temple, and was called to the bar in June 1891.
In London he met Theosophists, vegetarians and freethinkers. The city's spiritual marketplace, the subject of the book's religion chapter, shaped his politics too.
events: Gandhi enrols at the Inner Temple.

images.caption: Mohandas K. Gandhi as a law student in London
images.author: Unknown author

places.name: The Poland restaurant: Dowson's Cynara
places.summary: The little restaurant where Ernest Dowson played cards every night with the owner's daughter, the 'Cynara' of his poem.
text: The book tells how Dowson mooned over 'the young daughter of a Polish immigrant', playing cards with her every evening 'in her father's restaurant, until she married an Italian waiter'. She was Adelaide Foltinowicz. Dowson met her when she was about twelve, and his poem 'Non sum qualis eram bonae sub regno Cynarae' ('I have been faithful to thee, Cynara! in my fashion') came out of the affair.
Dowson died in 1900, aged thirty-two. He was one of the Rhymers whose lives Yeats called the 'tragic generation'.

places.name: Savage Club
places.summary: The Bohemian club of journalists and artists founded in 1857 by George Augustus Sala and friends.
text: The book introduces Sala, 'one of the most extraordinary figures of the period', as a founder of the Savage Club, and quotes at length his comic sketch of a club election: blackballing the snoring millionaire Bilberry and the cantankerous Admiral Grumps.
Clubs, the book says, were exclusive above all, each 'in its own way'. The Savage was exclusive in a Bohemian way, for writers, artists and performers rather than lords.

places.name: Garrick Club
places.summary: The club where actors and men of letters met: Irving, the Bancrofts, Pinero and Gilbert were members.
text: The book lists the Garrick among London's famous clubs. Founded in 1831 so that actors and gentlemen could meet as equals, it moved into this purpose-built clubhouse in 1864. Its members included Henry Irving, Squire Bancroft, Arthur Wing Pinero and W. S. Gilbert.

Acting became respectable in Wilde's London, as the book argues. Irving's knighthood in 1895, the first for an actor, was its high point, and the Garrick was where that respectability met the establishment.

images.caption: The Garrick Club, Illustrated London News, 1864
images.author: Unknown

places.name: The Strand
places.address: Strand, from Charing Cross to Temple Bar
places.summary: London's most congested street and its liveliest: theatres, newspapers, restaurants and Le Gallienne's 'iron lilies'.
text: The Strand appears all through the book. It calls it 'the most conspicuous traffic jam', an 'indirect, tortuous, obstructed and narrow lane' linking the City and Westminster. It was lined with theatres, restaurants and newspaper offices (the Illustrated London News at No. 198), and at night it was one of the West End's main places for prostitution.

Its gas lamps inspired Richard Le Gallienne's verses, quoted in the book: 'Lamp after lamp against the sky / Opens a sudden beaming eye... The iron lilies of the Strand.' Romano's, the Gaiety and the Savoy all stood on or just off it.

images.caption: The Strand in the nineteenth century
images.author: Anonymous Unknown author

places.name: Regent Street and the Quadrant
places.address: Regent Street, Piccadilly Circus to Oxford Circus
places.summary: Nash's unfinished royal way, the West End's shopping street and, under the Quadrant's curve, a place of night-time encounters.
text: The book tells how the Prince Regent asked John Nash in 1813 to drive a grand avenue north from Carlton House. 'London having a mind of its own', he got instead 'the essential, much rebuilt, south-north traffic artery of the West End'. It reproduces Francis Forster's 1897 painting of the Quadrant at night, gaslit and crowded with cabs. Liberty's, the Café Royal and Verrey's were all on Regent Street, and the shops stayed open late into the gaslit evening.

The Quadrant's curve, with Piccadilly next to it, was one of the West End's main places for street prostitution and, as Matt Cook shows, for men seeking men. The book's amateur beggar ended his day on Regent Street, where a woman beggar showed him the food and thirteen shillings she kept hidden in her dress.

images.caption: John Woods, The Quadrant, Regent Street
images.author: John Woods

places.name: Piccadilly Circus and 'Eros'
places.summary: Alfred Gilbert's Shaftesbury Memorial fountain (1893), the Angel of Christian Charity whom Londoners call Eros.
text: The book calls Gilbert's aluminium archer 'surely the most lovable and beloved' fountain in London. He was meant to be the Angel of Christian Charity, in memory of the reforming Lord Shaftesbury, 'but whom Londoners... mistake for Eros'. Soon after it was unveiled in 1893, Punch drew the missing arrow lodged in a passing cab driver's back.

Shaftesbury Avenue had just been cut through the slums to the circus (1886), which became the hub of the theatre district. Begging along Oxford Street, the book's undercover writer collected his last coppers from 'the last lingerer in the Circus'.

images.caption: In the Heart of Modern Babylon: Piccadilly Circus, 1896 stereograph
images.author: Strohmeyer & Wyman / Underwood & Underwood

places.name: Criterion Restaurant and Theatre
places.summary: A 'monster' restaurant palace serving two thousand dinners at a sitting, with a theatre underground.
text: The book quotes the Criterion's architect listing its dining rooms, grill room, buffet, smoking room, grand hall, cloakrooms 'and lastly a theatre', and an average of two thousand dinners served at once, sometimes 4,500. It is the book's example of the new restaurant culture, where an 1879 guidebook advised ladies shopping without an escort that they could lunch safely 'care being always taken to avoid passing through a drinking bar'.
In A Study in Scarlet Dr Watson hears of Sherlock Holmes for the first time standing at the Criterion Bar.

places.name: Trafalgar Square
places.summary: Jubilee processions, the 1886 unemployed riots and 'Bloody Sunday' in 1887.
text: The book reproduces the Illustrated London News's view of the 1887 Jubilee procession entering the square, 'the monumental aspect of London still dominates; the crowds seem to serve as decoration'. The square was also the city's political forum.

On 8 February 1886 a meeting of unemployed dockers and building workers here turned into a riot through St James's and Mayfair. On 'Bloody Sunday', 13 November 1887, police and troops broke up a banned demonstration. The book records two deaths and many arrests. Morris, Shaw and Annie Besant were among the marchers.
events: Unemployed riot spills out of Trafalgar Square.

images.caption: William Barnes Wollen, Bloody Sunday: the Life Guards holding Trafalgar Square, 1887
images.author: William Barnes Wollen

places.name: St James's Street and Clubland
places.address: St James's Street and Pall Mall
places.summary: The street of gentlemen's clubs, where the 1886 rioters smashed the windows and looted a wine shop.
text: The book names London's famous clubs: the Carlton, the Reform, the Garrick, the Marlborough, the Guards, the Army and Navy, White's and the Albemarle. Each was exclusive 'in its own way'. Most stood on Pall Mall and St James's Street.

On 8 February 1886 the East End met the West End here. The book reproduces the Illustrated London News's drawings of demonstrators on St James's Street and of rioters looting a wine shop, and quotes the Morning Post's report of shopkeepers barricading 'as if an invading army was expected'. Nearby, Lady Charlotte Bonham Carter remembered ruining her white suede shoes crossing to St James's Palace when no crossing sweeper was in sight.
events: Rioters smash club windows on St James's Street.

images.caption: Riots in the West End: the mob in St James's Street, February 1886
images.author: J. F. Weedon

places.name: Victoria Embankment
places.summary: Bazalgette's 'splendid thoroughfare' over the new sewers, where, General Booth found, the homeless slept on the benches.
text: The book quotes the Building News praising the Embankment as 'reared on foundations of Roman solidity'. It was meant to relieve the Strand, but traffic stayed there and the Embankment became 'a lovely place for a solitary walk'. A Kodak snapshot in the book shows a lady being pushed along it in a bath chair with her parasol and dog.

At two in the morning it was another place. William Booth's In Darkest England (1890), quoted at length in the book, counts the homeless sleeping 'by the score' on the benches under the plane trees between the Temple and Blackfriars, six to a seat, and on the stone abutments out of the wind.
events: Booth's In Darkest England describes the Embankment sleepers.

images.caption: John Atkinson Grimshaw, Reflections on the Thames, Westminster, 1880
images.author: John Atkinson Grimshaw

places.name: Tower Bridge
places.summary: Opened in 1894: modern steel engineering dressed in Gothic stone.
text: The book uses Tower Bridge as its example of the age's nostalgia. It was built 'at about the same time as the Eiffel Tower, and just as advanced in its steel construction', but 'disguised in Gothic masonry'. Work began in 1886 and the bridge opened in June 1894.
The same mood, the book says, produced Morris's Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings and the revival of medieval crafts. London built for the future while dressing in the past.
events: Tower Bridge opened by the Prince of Wales.

places.name: Stockwell: the first electric tube
places.address: Stockwell, terminus of the City and South London Railway
places.summary: The southern end of the world's first deep-level electric railway (1890), and where the Prince of Wales caught his train.
text: The book records that 'a year after the first London County Council was installed', London's first electric underground line opened between the City and Stockwell, in November 1890. (It calls it the 'two-penny tube', a name that really belonged to the Central London Railway of 1900.) It also tells, perhaps too generously, the story of the American financier Charles Tyson Yerkes and London's later tubes.
The book also shows the Prince of Wales, with umbrella and binoculars, setting off by rail from Stockwell station.
events: City and South London Railway opened.

images.caption: Borough station on the new City & South London Railway, the world's first deep-level electric tube (Illustrated London News, 8 November 1890)
images.author: The Illustrated London News

places.name: Baker Street: the Metropolitan Railway
places.summary: The world's first underground railway (1863), whose cheap workmen's trains pushed London outward.
text: The book reproduces the 1863 maiden trip of the Metropolitan line and the 'cut and cover' trenches that built it. It notes the subsidised workmen's trains at the beginning and end of the working day, 'to encourage low-income families to move out of the slums into the new suburbs'.

The Underground, built between 1863 and 1914, 'brought the new suburbs within reach of the center and people at the center within reach of the cricket and football fields on the perimeter'. Sherlock Holmes's fictional address was round the corner.

places.name: Kingsbury-Neasden
places.summary: The Metropolitan Railway's yards and works in the countryside north of London.
text: The book reproduces a Kodak photograph of a train entering Kingsbury-Neasden station, 'to the north of London, where the Metropolitan Railroad yards were located'. The Metropolitan opened the station in 1880 as it pushed out into Middlesex, and built works and a workers' village here.
This was the start of 'Metro-land', with fields turned into commuter suburbs within a generation.

places.name: Lots Road Power Station
places.summary: Yerkes's coal-fired power station for the tubes, built on Whistler's and Turner's stretch of river.
text: The book says Whistler 'led the outcry over the ugly, smoke-belching power station Yerkes placed at the precise bend of the Thames that Turner had made famous'. Built in 1902–05 to power the Underground, Lots Road stood on the reach of the river below Battersea Bridge painted in the Nocturnes.
It is outside Wilde's years (Whistler died in 1903), but the book uses it to show the clash between art and technology at the heart of its argument.

places.name: Imperial Institute
places.address: Exhibition Road / Imperial College (Queen's Tower survives)
places.summary: Collcutt's Jubilee monument to the Empire (1887–93), of which only the tower survives.
text: Conceived for the 1887 Jubilee to house exhibitions and research on the colonies, the Institute was designed by T. E. Collcutt in a mixture of French, Flemish and Spanish styles. Tennyson hoped it would 'speak to the centuries', and the book quotes the wit who asked whether 'the centuries understand Esperanto'.
It is the book's emblem of late-Victorian eclecticism, a 'compendium of world architecture'. Except for the Queen's Tower, it 'did not survive the Empire'.

places.name: Royal Courts of Justice
places.summary: G. E. Street's sprawling Gothic Law Courts, opened by the Queen in 1882.
text: The book lists the Law Courts, 'all fairy-tale picturesqueness by architect G. E. Street', among the landmarks of High Victorian building. They opened in December 1882 and brought the superior courts from Westminster Hall to the Strand.

Watching eminent Victorians make fools of themselves in court, the book says, was one of the period's most popular entertainments. Whistler, Ruskin, Maskelyne, the Prince of Wales in the Tranby Croft case and, finally, Wilde all provided it.

images.caption: The Royal Courts of Justice, photographed by George Washington Wilson
images.author: George Washington Wilson

places.name: New Scotland Yard
places.summary: Norman Shaw's 'dour police palace' of 1890, headquarters of the Metropolitan Police.
text: The book counts Norman Shaw's granite-and-brick building among 'the conspicuous landmarks of High Victorian'. The Met moved in during 1890, after the Jack the Ripper investigations had damaged its reputation. A female torso had been found in the building's foundations in 1888.

The book shows the bobby as a reassuring presence on the street, helping drunken gentlemen home in Charles Keene's sketch, and also as a force ordered against crowds in Trafalgar Square. Wilde was taken to Scotland Yard after his arrest before being charged at Bow Street.
events: Metropolitan Police move to New Scotland Yard.
Wilde brought here after his arrest.

places.name: National Liberal Club
places.summary: Waterhouse's tiled palace for Gladstonian Liberals (1887), the book's example of 'Period Architecture'.
text: The book illustrates the National Liberal Club as typical 'Period Architecture'. Alfred Waterhouse's riverside clubhouse, opened in 1887, was a palace of faience and marble for a party that was trying to bring in a wider membership than the old clubs allowed.
It gave Gladstone's party, and the radical Liberals the book discusses, such as Labouchère and Bradlaugh, a West End address.

places.name: The Elephant and Castle
places.summary: The old coaching inn at south London's great road junction, rebuilt in the 1890s as a 'polychrome whimsy'.
text: The book twice illustrates the Elephant and Castle pub: as an Arts and Crafts design and among High Victorian landmarks, 'once a coaching house, rebuilt in the 1890s into a polychrome whimsy'.
It also stands for the book's 'golden age' of the pub, with mirrors, mahogany and cut glass, one pub for every 345 Londoners, the place where the classes met and the working man waited for his bus.

places.name: Whitehall
places.summary: The imperial ministries: the Colonial Office, the Admiralty, the War Office, and an army of civil servants.
text: The book describes how 'the Colonial Office, the Admiralty, the War Office, the Ministry of Education, and dozens of other bureaucracies built monumental new offices around Whitehall'. By 1900 London had 160,000 civil servants.
In the book's account of Cleveland Street, 'someone in Whitehall' warned Lord Arthur Somerset in time for him to escape.

places.name: Houses of Parliament
places.summary: Where Bradlaugh was locked in the Clock Tower, Lords heard evidence on child prostitution, and the Labouchère amendment became law.
text: The book opens with Beerbohm's memory of 'the incomparable Parliament of 1880': Gladstone triumphant, Parnell 'pale, deadly, mysterious', Randolph Churchill's Fourth Party, and the atheist Charles Bradlaugh dragged down the stone steps. Refusing to swear the religious oath, Bradlaugh was imprisoned in the Clock Tower, re-elected again and again, and finally took his seat in 1886.

In 1881 a House of Lords committee heard Superintendent Joseph Dunlap describe children of twelve soliciting in his division; the book prints the exchange. In August 1885, after Stead's 'Maiden Tribute', Parliament passed the Criminal Law Amendment Act. Late one night Henry Labouchère added a clause making 'gross indecency' between men, 'in public or private', punishable by two years' hard labour. The book notes that 'or private' was 'an invitation for blackmail'. Wilde was convicted under it.
events: Bradlaugh refuses the oath and is held in the Clock Tower.
Lords committee on the protection of young girls.
Labouchère amendment added to the Criminal Law Amendment Bill.

images.caption: 'Lib' (Liborio Prosperi), The Lobby of the House of Commons, 1886
images.author: Liborio Prosperi

places.name: Westminster Abbey
places.summary: Scene of Victoria's Golden Jubilee thanksgiving in 1887, and Irving's burial in 1905.
text: The book reproduces the Illustrated London News's 1887 Jubilee picture, in which 'the crowds almost vanish beneath the overpowering image of Westminster Abbey, representing the enduring and unchangeable monarchy'. The Queen was Head of the Church as well as the State.
The book notes that Sir Henry Irving was buried here in 1905, an honour that shows how respectable acting had become.

images.caption: William Ewart Lockhart, Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee Service, Westminster Abbey, 1887
images.author: William Ewart Lockhart

places.name: Buckingham Palace
places.summary: Royal garden parties, court balls the Queen never attended, and Tom Thumb's audiences.
text: The book reproduces the Golden Jubilee garden party of 29 June 1887 and describes the annual court balls of the Season, 'although the Queen, finding no amusement in dancing, never attended'.

Earlier, in 1844, P. T. Barnum's six-year-old 'General Tom Thumb' was received here three times. Punch scolded the Queen for showering honours on an American 'whose astounding genius it is to measure in his boots five-and-twenty inches'.

images.caption: Frederick Sargent, The Garden Party at Buckingham Palace, 1887
images.author: Frederick Sargent

places.name: Covent Garden Market
places.summary: Inigo Jones's piazza turned vegetable market, where Wilde's Lord Arthur Savile wandered at dawn.
text: The book returns to Covent Garden several times. In 'Lord Arthur Savile's Crime', Wilde's hero watches the carts arrive at dawn, with vegetables 'like masses of jade against the morning sky', and wonders what the carters knew of London's 'splendour and its shame'. The book uses that phrase for its own chapters.

It tells the history of the piazza, laid out by Inigo Jones for the Earl of Bedford in the 1630s and the 'prototype for the London Square', later taken over by market traders. It also recalls that Shaw opened Pygmalion under the portico of St Paul's church here, with Higgins placing Eliza Doolittle's accent in Lisson Grove.

images.caption: John Thomson, Covent Garden Flower Women, 1877
images.author: John Thomson (1837-1921)

places.name: Harrods
places.summary: With Whiteley's, the greatest of the department stores in the book's account of shopping as entertainment.
text: The book names Harrods in Knightsbridge and Whiteley's in Westbourne Grove as 'the biggest' department stores. A fire in 1883 forced Harrods to rebuild larger, and in 1898 it installed London's first escalator, with brandy served at the top for nervous customers.
The book argues that for the new middle class shopping had become 'a form of entertainment', and that store clerks paid for the late opening hours by working as much as eighty hours a week.
events: Harrods burns and is rebuilt larger.

places.name: Whiteley's
places.summary: William Whiteley's 'Universal Provider', where, the book says, Wilde shopped.
text: Whiteley's started as a draper in the 1860s. 'By the time Oscar Wilde shopped there', the book says, it sold 'just about everything anybody could hope to get out of life short of love, from perfume to pianos'. It had a ladies' retiring room, theatre ticket agency, bank, refreshment room and dry cleaning.
The book reproduces G. W. Joy's painting The Bayswater Omnibus, whose passengers, from a smart young woman to a working man, are on their way to the shops of this new middle-class district.

images.caption: George William Joy, The Bayswater Omnibus, 1895
images.author: George W. Joy

places.name: Holborn Restaurant
places.summary: A huge 'culinary palace' with fifteen private dining rooms and a grill room for family outings.
text: The book cites the Holborn among the new restaurant palaces, with decor ranging from 'fancy French' gilding to Venetian Gothic rooms and Wagnerian halls. In 1888, it notes, a father, mother, governess and four children could dine in its Grill Room for fifteen shillings.
Such places sold a taste of upper-class luxury to the office workers whose rising incomes, the book argues, were remaking the centre of London.

images.caption: Daily menu of the Holborn Restaurant
images.author: Scan by NYPL

places.name: Northumberland Avenue hotels
places.address: Northumberland Avenue: the Grand, the Victoria, the Metropole
places.summary: A new avenue of six-hundred-room 'monster' hotels, with semaphore signals instead of servants' bells.
text: Cut through the grounds of Northumberland House in 1876, the avenue filled with the Grand (1880), the Victoria (1887) and the Metropole (1885). The book quotes the Building News on the Metropole: a vestibule copied from the Louvre's Gallery of Apollo, a 'Marie Antoinette chamber', some six hundred bedrooms, and a little semaphore outside each door that raised its arm when a guest rang the electric bell.
These were hotels for 'the idlers of the globe', as one writer called the international steamship set, for whom the West End was a 'pleasure lounge'.

places.name: Harley Street
places.summary: Where 'most of the good doctors practiced', out of reach of the working families who bought cures from street sellers.
text: The book sets J. W. Thompson's photograph of a 'street doctor' against Harley Street, 'where most of the good doctors practiced'. Working-class families could not afford to travel there, 'let alone be treated'. They bought patent medicines from pedlars and tried to cure tuberculosis with 'cough preventatives'.

It is one of the book's many pairings of West End privilege with the medicine of the poor, alongside its advertisement for the Electropathic Belt and its account of 'phossy jaw' in the match factories.

images.caption: John Thomson, Street Doctors, from Street Life in London, 1877
images.author: John Thomson

places.name: Park Lane
places.summary: The richest street in London, with horse buses running past its mansions.
text: The book notes that the dense horse-bus network ran 'even such elegant residential streets as Park Lane', and reproduces photographs of the buses. In Sala's sketch of a club election the most eligible candidate is a man of forty-seven 'with a delightful house in Park Lane'.
Lillie Langtry's first London home was in Norfolk Street, just off Park Lane. Wilde called there often in his first London years.

places.name: Purrett Road, Plumstead
places.summary: Rows of new terraced houses for Woolwich Arsenal workers, the book's picture of the suburb.
text: The book's photograph of Purrett Road in the 1890s shows uniform two-storey terraces with tiny front gardens. It comments that suburbs gave workers 'space and comforts they could not afford in the center city', but that 'but for a pub at the corner, there were few public amenities'.
It quotes the Building News complaining in 1884 of the 'dull and wearying sameness' of suburbs, 'as if individuals had tastes precisely the same'.

places.name: Walthamstow and Tottenham: workmen's-train suburbs
places.summary: Working-class suburbs built on the cheap fares that the 1883 Cheap Trains Act forced on the railways.
text: The book explains that the Cheap Trains Act of 1883 required the railways to run reduced-fare workmen's trains, and that suburbs 'like Tottenham and Walthamstow' were built on them. A year later the chairman of London Tramways boasted: 'We have relieved London of an immense number of poor people by carrying them out to the suburbs.'
The book praises the suburbs for decent housing but blames them for lengthening the journey to work and fixing the class system more rigidly in single-class streets.

images.caption: Charles Booth's Map Descriptive of London Poverty, 1898–99, sheet 22
images.author: Charles Booth

places.name: West India Docks and the Great Dock Strike
places.summary: The port that made London rich and kept its workers poor, and the 1889 strike for the 'dockers' tanner'.
text: The book describes the docks drawing 'vast numbers of people from all over the world'. Casual labourers were hired by the day at the dock gates, and women laundered and cooked for sailors. Railways, steamships and mechanised cranes were cutting the work, and fog or snow could stop it altogether, bringing 'serious hunger'.

The London Dock Strike of August 1889 began at the West India Docks. Led by Ben Tillett, John Burns and Tom Mann, the dockers held out for a month and won sixpence an hour. The book says the strike 'backed up the growing clamor with a show of real power'.

images.caption: Dock labourers' mass meeting during the Great Strike, 7 September 1889
images.author: Unknown author

images.caption: Strikers on the East India Dock Road, 1889
images.author: Unknown author

places.name: Fore Street, Lambeth
places.summary: A riverside slum whose photograph the book uses to show housing barely changed since Dickens.
text: The book reproduces a photograph of Fore Street, Lambeth. It comments that London 'suffered worse housing conditions than other English cities' and that the slums Dickens described in the 1840s and '50s 'had changed little by the end of the century'.
The narrow riverside lanes of Lambeth, between the potteries, wharves and the lunatic hospital of Bedlam, were cleared for the Albert Embankment and later council housing. The marker is approximate.

places.name: Seven Dials
places.summary: The St Giles rookery where, the book says, even the police feared to patrol, and the 'Dialonians' waited outside the station.
text: The book reproduces a Guildhall Library view of Seven Dials, 'so dangerous that even bobbies feared for their safety'. (It places the district 'in the East End'; in fact it lies in the West End, beside Covent Garden.) In 1881 Superintendent Dunlap told the Lords about the 'Dialonians' he saw outside his station, including a girl of about thirteen with rings on every finger, waiting to see 'her man' go down in the police van.
Dickens had written about the Dials in the 1830s. Charing Cross Road and Shaftesbury Avenue were cut through the rookery in the 1880s, scattering its people into other crowded streets.

images.caption: Gustave Doré, Dudley Street, Seven Dials, 1872
images.author: https://wellcomeimages.org/indexplus/obf_images/9c/42/386f773494bdbe7e26f89ea735d2.jpg Gallery: http

places.name: Bartholomew Close, Smithfield
places.summary: Beside London's meat market, a byway known for stolen goods and prostitution.
text: The book's photograph of Bartholomew Close shows the old houses near Smithfield, 'the center of London's meat trade', which it calls 'a place of illegal traffic in stolen goods and prostitution'.

Smithfield's great new market halls (1868) stood next to medieval alleys and the hospital of St Bartholomew. It was the kind of contrast the book keeps finding, and the site of the old Bartholomew Fair whose peep shows its diversions chapter describes.

images.caption: John Wykeham Archer, Room in the Coach and Horses, Bartholomew Close, 1851
images.author: John Wykeham Archer

places.name: Petticoat Lane
places.summary: The Sunday market at the heart of Jewish Whitechapel, photographed for Dr Barnardo to show the horrors of poverty.
text: The book reproduces a photograph of Petticoat Lane used by Dr Barnardo's Home for Working and Destitute Lads 'to document the horrors of poverty'. It calls the lane 'the center of commercial life in Whitechapel'.
Beatrice Potter's study of the Jewish East End, quoted in the book, follows a newly arrived family to the comfortable home of an orange dealer in Mitre Street, 'near to Petticoat Lane'.

images.caption: Petticoat Lane market, 1920s
images.author: George Grantham Bain Collection (Library of Congress)

places.name: Houndsditch
places.summary: The old-clothes quarter where an undercover journalist bought his beggar's 'rig-out'.
text: The book prints an 1884 account by an 'amateur street-beggar' who bought his disguise from a Jewish dealer 'in the neighbourhood of Houndsditch': a buttonless tweed coat, faded trousers 'as jagged at the extremities as the outline of the Alps', a greasy slouch hat and hopeless boots.
He then begged along Oxford Street for six hours and made one and tenpence. Women, he found, gave more readily than men, and elderly gentlemen looked round for a policeman.
events: The 'amateur street-beggar' buys his disguise here.

places.name: Poor Jews' Temporary Shelter, Leman Street
places.summary: Refuge for Jewish immigrants landing from Hamburg, beset at the river stairs by 'runners' and swindlers.
text: The book prints Beatrice Potter's account of a Hamburg boat steaming up the Thames with Polish and Russian Jews fleeing the pogroms, and the confusion at the landing stage: dock loungers jeering, 'runners' grabbing bundles and selling bogus tickets to America, and a little man from the Hebrew Ladies' Protective Society calling to the newcomers to go to the Poor Jews' Temporary Shelter in Leman Street.

Potter traces the 'greener' from sweated labour to a model dwelling, a fur-wearing wife and 'season tickets for the People's Palace'. The book notes the antisemitism the immigration provoked, including during the Ripper panic.

images.caption: Russian refugees in the Poor Jews' Temporary Shelter, Leman Street, 1891
images.author: Ellen Gertrude Cohen

places.name: Commercial Street and Toynbee Hall
places.summary: The open-air labour market for Jewish tailors, and the university settlement where Oxford men came to live among the poor.
text: In Beatrice Potter's account, quoted in the book, the immigrant who has learnt his trade 'can sell his skill in the open market at the corner of Commercial Street'.

On the same street Canon Samuel Barnett opened Toynbee Hall in 1884, a settlement where university graduates lived and taught in the East End. Seth Koven's Slumming examines its mixture of social idealism, curiosity and erotic attraction across class lines. The book quotes the Bitter Cry of Outcast London (1883), the pamphlet that helped start the movement.

places.name: Christ Church, Spitalfields
places.summary: Hawksmoor's church, whose churchyard seats were an outdoor bedroom for the homeless.
text: General Booth, quoted in the book, found 'al fresco lodgings' in 'the seats outside Spitalfields Church', and two women making a home in a shop doorway in nearby Liverpool Street. The churchyard was known locally as 'Itchy Park'.
Hawksmoor's tower looked down on the common lodging houses of Flower and Dean Street and Dorset Street, where most of the Ripper's victims had lived.

places.name: Bedfordbury
places.summary: A slum alley off St Martin's Lane where, Booth reported, a homeless young woman died after being drenched as she slept in a van.
text: The book prints General Booth's story of a young woman who slept in a van in Bedfordbury. Men who knew her habits threw a bucket of water over her, she fell ill, and a coroner's jury found that the soaking 'only hastened her death, which was due, in plain English, to starvation'.

Bedfordbury lay a few minutes' walk from the theatres of St Martin's Lane and the Strand. Peabody Trust model dwellings replaced much of it, the kind of 'worthy dwellings' Gladstone praised in his reply to Tennyson.

places.name: Lisson Grove
places.summary: Where Shaw's Eliza Doolittle was born and where the real 'Lily' of Stead's 'Maiden Tribute', Eliza Armstrong, was bought for £5.
text: The book quotes Pygmalion: Higgins places the flower girl in Lisson Grove by her accent, and Eliza protests that it 'wasn't fit for a pig to live in; and I had to pay four-and-six a week'.

Judith Walkowitz identifies the real child of Stead's 'Maiden Tribute' (the book's 'Lily') as Eliza Armstrong, thirteen, of Charles Street, Lisson Grove. Her mother sold her to a procuress for £5. When the truth came out, Stead was convicted of abducting her. The book reprints his account of a midwife's 'certificate', chloroform, and the child crying 'There's a man in the room!'
events: Eliza Armstrong taken from Lisson Grove by Stead's agent.

places.name: Hoxton
places.summary: A byword for poverty and crime, and Higgins's guess for the Sarcastic Bystander.
text: In the scene from Pygmalion the book quotes, Higgins guesses 'Hoxton' for a bystander's home. The book uses the scene to show that London's neighbourhoods were 'so distinct in their character and makeup that they even had their own dialects'.
Charles Booth's poverty maps coloured much of Hoxton dark blue and black, the lowest classes. His investigators reckoned it one of the leading criminal quarters of the city.

places.name: Dr Barnardo's Home, Stepney Causeway
places.summary: Barnardo's Home for Working and Destitute Lads, whose before-and-after photographs raised funds for child rescue.
text: The book reproduces Barnardo's photographs: 'Once a Little Vagrant' and 'Now a Little Workman', crippled boys in uniform, and the case of six-year-old Emma Cook, admitted in 1887. These were images sold to raise money and, the book notes, carefully staged. Barnardo's admission photographs are now studied as evidence of how charity looked at the poor.
Stepney was also sweatshop country. The book quotes the seamstress Rachel Silver going round Stepney 'looking into house windows to see if there were any hands wanted'.

images.caption: Disabled boys in the yard of Barnardo's Stepney Causeway home
images.author: Barnardo, Thomas John

places.name: People's Palace
places.address: Mile End Road (now Queen Mary University of London)
places.summary: The East End's palace of culture and recreation, opened by the Queen in 1887.
text: Inspired by Walter Besant's novel All Sorts and Conditions of Men, the People's Palace opened in May 1887 with the Queen's Hall for concerts, a library, swimming baths and technical classes. Beatrice Potter's prospering immigrant in the book 'thinks seriously of season tickets for the People's Palace'.
It belongs to the book's account of 'rational recreation', culture as a remedy for drink, and to the period's hope that institutions could civilise the East End.
events: Queen Victoria opens the People's Palace.

images.caption: The Reading Room of the People's Palace, c. 1890
images.author: Unknown author

places.name: George Yard: Martha Tabram
places.summary: Where Martha Tabram was found stabbed on 7 August 1888. The book counts her the first of the series, 'later understood not to be'.
text: The book begins its account of the Whitechapel murders with Martha Tabram, found in George Yard Buildings on 7 August 1888 with dozens of stab wounds. It notes that she was 'later understood not to be of the series' because she was not mutilated.

Hallie Rubenhold's The Five has since challenged the book's labelling of all the victims as prostitutes, a label taken from police and press assumptions. The women had many ways of getting by in the lodging-house economy.

places.name: Buck's Row: Mary Ann Nichols
places.summary: Mary Ann Nichols was found here on 31 August 1888, when, in the book's words, 'the Jack the Ripper serial officially began'.
text: Mary Ann 'Polly' Nichols, a printer's former wife who had lived in workhouses and lodging houses, was found in Buck's Row in the early hours of 31 August 1888. The book follows the Illustrated Police News's lurid pictures. Its drawings of the killer changed over the autumn, from a caricature of an Eastern European Jew to a 'degenerate' in a workman's bowler, and finally to an upper-class fop with a fur collar.
The book argues that the murders 'brought the plight of the East End slum dwellers to the rest of London', and also relieved middle-class fears by locating sexual violence among the 'lower orders'.

images.caption: The Illustrated London News, 22 September 1888: the Whitechapel murders
images.author: Henry Charles Seppings Wright

places.name: 29 Hanbury Street: Annie Chapman
places.summary: Annie Chapman was killed in the back yard here on 8 September 1888.
text: The book says Chapman's body was found 'in back of Dr. Thomas Barnardo's children's asylum'. In fact it was the yard of a lodging house at 29 Hanbury Street, close to Barnardo's premises. Her womb was removed, the coroner said, 'by an expert', which fed theories that the killer was a doctor.
Rubenhold's research recovers Chapman's life as a coachman's wife from Windsor whose family fell apart through drink and grief.

places.name: Berner Street: Elizabeth Stride
places.summary: Elizabeth Stride was found in Dutfield's Yard on 30 September 1888, the night of the 'double event'.
text: Stride, a Swedish immigrant, was found beside the International Working Men's Educational Club, a Jewish socialist club, in the early hours of 30 September 1888. The location stoked the antisemitism the book describes.
Less than an hour later another woman was killed in Mitre Square. The book calls the night the one on which 'Jack struck twice'.

images.caption: The discovery in Berner Street, Penny Illustrated Paper, 6 October 1888
images.author: Unknown author

places.name: Mitre Square: Catherine Eddowes
places.summary: Catherine Eddowes was killed here inside the City boundary on 30 September 1888.
text: Because Mitre Square lay just inside the City of London, the Eddowes murder brought the City Police into the hunt alongside the Metropolitan Police. Nearby, a chalked message on a wall in Goulston Street about 'the Juwes' was rubbed out on police orders for fear of anti-Jewish riots.
The book reproduces the Illustrated Police News pages, whose pictures sold the story across the country.

places.name: Miller's Court, Dorset Street: Mary Jane Kelly
places.summary: The last canonical victim, Mary Jane Kelly, was found in her room here on 9 November 1888.
text: The book records that the remains of Mary Jane Kelly were found in Miller's Court, off Dorset Street, on 9 November 1888, the day of the Lord Mayor's Show. Dorset Street was reckoned the worst street in London, a row of common lodging houses.

'All of London was in a panic', the book says, 'even though the murders were clearly limited to the most desolate whores in the most poverty-stricken area of the city'. The phrasing is very much of 1987, and Rubenhold's work now questions it.

places.name: Bryant & May match factory
places.summary: Where the matchgirls struck in 1888 against fines, low pay and 'phossy jaw'.
text: The book describes the 'phos' girls without jaws or fingers, their bones eaten by white phosphorus, begging in the streets, and girls working 8 am to 9 pm for seven to eleven shillings a week. It names a 'Victoria Match Factory' employing over a thousand women. James Greenwood's account of two shivering under-age 'hands' outside a north London factory follows.

The best-known case is Bryant & May in Bow. In July 1888 Annie Besant exposed conditions there in 'White Slavery in London', and some 1,400 women and girls walked out and won. Besant is a recurring figure in the book, as Bradlaugh's co-defendant, a socialist and a Theosophist.

images.caption: A page from the matchgirls' strike register, 1888
images.author: Annie Besant and Herbert Burrows

places.name: Bluegate Fields: the opium dens
places.address: Bluegate Fields, off Ratcliffe Highway, Shadwell
places.summary: The opium rooms of 'Tiger Bay' that journalists visited, and where Dorian Gray goes to 'buy oblivion'.
text: The book reprints James Greenwood's visit to an opium master in Bluegate Fields, 'Tiger Bay', with 'tigresses' lolling at their doors. Expecting a mandarin, he found 'a shabby, shambling, middle-aged Chinaman' with a lame leg. He took two pulls on a bamboo pipe, was violently sick, and paid half a crown to escape into 'the free and delicious air of Shadwell'.

Dorian Gray takes a hansom east through the fog to just such 'dens of horror' near the docks. Wilde's novel and Greenwood's reporting share the same fantasy of the East End: dangerous, foreign and addictive. Doré's engraving of a Bluegate Fields opium smoker is the best-known image of it.
events: Dorian Gray's visit to the opium den published.

images.caption: Gustave Doré, an opium den in east London, from London: A Pilgrimage (1872)
images.author: Gustave Doré

places.name: Salvation Army headquarters
places.summary: General William Booth's 'army' made war on sin with brass bands, street theatre and rescue homes.
text: The book quotes the Saturday Review on a Salvation Army meeting roaring 'with fire and blood', and a converted Welsh shoemaker announcing himself 'a Hallelujah pastor at Whitechapel'. The Army moved its headquarters here in 1881.

Booth's In Darkest England and the Way Out (1890) supplies some of the book's most vivid evidence on homelessness and prostitution. His son Bramwell set up Stead's purchase of Eliza Armstrong to win support for raising the age of consent.
events: Salvation Army moves to Queen Victoria Street.

images.caption: General William Booth by Spy, Vanity Fair, 1882
images.author: Leslie Ward

places.name: Metropolitan Tabernacle
places.summary: Spurgeon's Baptist 'megachurch', seating over six thousand, the largest Protestant church in London.
text: The book reproduces a portrait of Charles Haddon Spurgeon, who 'recognized that an upper-class church had little to offer to the common people'. His Tabernacle, built in 1861 behind a giant classical portico, held over six thousand people and was filled every Sunday until his death in 1892.
Spurgeon stands for the book's argument that Nonconformity and evangelical showmanship reached Londoners whom the established Church had lost.

images.caption: The Metropolitan Tabernacle
images.author: The original uploader was Secretlondon at English Wikipedia .

places.name: 19 Avenue Road: the Theosophists
places.summary: Annie Besant's house, which became the London headquarters of Madame Blavatsky's Theosophical Society.
text: The book describes Theosophy as 'the rage' and notes that Constance Wilde joined. Annie Besant, set to review Blavatsky's Secret Doctrine by W. T. Stead, converted, to the horror of Bradlaugh and the amusement of Shaw, who offered to be her mahatma. In 1890 she gave her house here to Blavatsky, who died in it in May 1891.
Alex Owen's history of the occult shows how Theosophy, the Golden Dawn (which Constance also joined) and spiritualism offered educated women spiritual authority the churches denied them.

places.name: Farm Street Church
places.summary: The Jesuit church to which Wilde wrote on the day of his release, asking to make a retreat. He was refused.
text: The book notes Wilde's lifelong pull towards Roman Catholicism: he called it 'the fowler's snare' at Oxford, hoped it might make him give up his 'two great gods, Money and Ambition', and was received into the Church on his deathbed in Paris in 1900.

On 19 May 1897, at Headlam's house, Wilde wrote to the Jesuits at Farm Street asking to go on retreat for six months. The reply said he could not be accepted on impulse and must wait a year. He wept, and left for France that night.
events: Wilde's request for a retreat refused.

images.caption: Farm Street Church (Church of the Immaculate Conception)
images.author: CVB

places.name: Royal Arsenal, Woolwich
places.summary: The armaments works whose workers had their own hearse, their own football club and nearby, in Booth's telling, a trap for the friendless.
text: The book's pictures of Woolwich include the official hearse reserved for workers at the munitions factories ('Funerals were the most spectacular religious events'). Workers founded Woolwich Arsenal FC in 1886, which became Arsenal, one of the works teams the book counts alongside West Ham, founded as Thames Ironworks.
General Booth's case files, quoted in the book, tell of a friendless girl discharged from hospital who was befriended in the street and led to a brothel 'in the very lowest part of Woolwich'.
events: Workers found the club that becomes Arsenal.

places.name: Hyde Park and Rotten Row
places.summary: The Season's parade ground: courtesans on horseback, American heiresses 'in the Row', and the bicycle craze of 1895.
text: The book describes crowds lining the Row to watch the famous courtesans ride, Catherine 'Skittles' Walters above all (it reproduces her portrait). It quotes Wilde on the American girls of the Season, whose greetings 'in a drawing room or in the Row' were 'like a series of exploding crackers'.

By the mid-1890s the middle classes had taken to bicycles here. The book reproduces a Hyde Park scene of 1895, 'while the nobility showed off its thoroughbred horses, the middle class showed off its bicycles', and quotes a fashion writer admiring Mrs W. H. Grenfell, all in soft green, gliding 'through the throng in Hyde Park'.
events: The bicycle craze reaches Hyde Park.

places.name: Battersea Park
places.summary: 'Always the most fashionable venue' for lady cyclists, and the scene of Paul Martin's 1892 fair photographs.
text: The book quotes Mrs Harcourt Williamson: 'At Battersea, which was always the most fashionable venue', Lady William Nevill rode in navy blue with a white sailor collar, and smart women had their machines painted in their own colours, green with primrose lines, or crimson and blue.

It also reproduces Paul Martin's photograph of a lemonade stand at the Battersea Park fair in 1892. The book treats women's cycling as a revolution in dress and mobility: 'not a revolt, it is a revolution'.
events: Paul Martin photographs the Battersea Park fair.

places.name: Victoria Park
places.summary: The East End's 'People's Park', where Paul Martin photographed three little girls.
text: Laid out in the 1840s to give the East End its own lungs, Victoria Park had a lake, a bathing pond and a speakers' corner. The book reproduces Paul Martin's candid photograph of three little girls here, and calls London's parks 'the lungs of the city', used 'by young and old, rich and poor'.
Martin's pictures, taken with a hidden camera, are set in the book against staged studio scenes such as 'The Proposal' (1888), sold as home decorations.

places.name: Earl's Court exhibition grounds
places.summary: Site of popular exhibitions from 1887; the book shows an al fresco tea party at its pavilion in 1885.
text: The book reproduces Paul Martin's photograph of an open-air tea party at the Earl's Court pavilion in 1885, an early piece of candid street photography. From 1887 the grounds between the railway lines hosted the American Exhibition, Buffalo Bill's Wild West show and a series of national exhibitions, and in 1895 a giant Ferris wheel.
Earl's Court was also one of the new neighbourhoods the book names, with its own character and dialect, in its passage on Pygmalion.
