events: Paul Martin photographs tea at the pavilion.
American Exhibition and Buffalo Bill open.

places.name: Lord's Cricket Ground
places.summary: When W. G. Grace was not out at lunch, the clubs emptied and the road to St John's Wood 'tinkled' with hansom cabs.
text: The book devotes pages to cricket as the mirror of English virtue, from Newbolt's 'Play up! play up! and play the game!' to a clergyman's Cricket Field of the Christian Life. It quotes Neville Cardus on W. G. Grace: when Grace was reported not out at Lord's at lunch, 'the London clubs emptied, and the road to St. John's Wood all afternoon was tinkling with... the hansom cab'.
Lord's was the home of the Marylebone Cricket Club, which governed cricket and, the book notes, real tennis too. The first Wimbledon even paused for the Eton–Harrow match here.
events: Grace, aged 47, scores a thousand runs in May.

images.caption: W. G. Grace playing forward, from Ranjitsinhji's Jubilee Book of Cricket, 1897
images.author: Credit: "From photo by E. Hawkins & Co., Brighton"

places.name: Kennington Oval
places.summary: Surrey's cricket ground, scene of the first Test in England (1880) and of FA Cup finals until 1892.
text: The book's sport chapter sets out the quarrel between amateurs and professionals in football and the shift of power from London's gentlemen's clubs to the northern works teams. The Oval was where it played out: every FA Cup final but one between 1872 and 1892 was held here, until the crowds outgrew it and the final moved to the Crystal Palace.
In 1880 the Oval also staged the first cricket Test match in England, with Grace scoring a century.
events: Last FA Cup final at the Oval.

places.name: All England Croquet and Lawn Tennis Club
places.summary: Where the first lawn tennis championship was played in 1877, breaking for two days for the Eton–Harrow match.
text: The book tells how Major Clopton Wingfield patented 'Sphairistikè' as a garden game, and how in 1875 the All England Croquet Club set aside a lawn for it. The first championship in 1877 'took a two-day break, in keeping with sporting priorities', for the Eton–Harrow cricket match at Lord's. Spencer Gore won by volleying; the next year a tea planter beat him with lobs.
The book reproduces The Graphic's 1881 view of the championships and notes that tennis, like archery and later cycling, became a sport for women too.

places.name: Putney: the Boat Race
places.summary: The Thames at Putney, start of the Oxford and Cambridge Boat Race and of the rowing regattas the book illustrates.
text: The book notes that rowing 'attracted many fine athletes as well as enthusiastic crowds', and reproduces a Thames regatta and its onlookers. The University Boat Race from Putney to Mortlake drew vast crowds along the towpaths each spring.
It sits alongside the book's other sports of the age, from Captain Webb's Channel swim of 1875 to the mountaineering of Justice Wills, who climbed the Wetterhorn before he sentenced Wilde.

images.caption: The University Boat Race on the Thames, 1869
images.author: Currier & Ives.

places.name: The Crystal Palace, Sydenham
places.summary: Paxton's glasshouse on its hill: concerts since 1855, fireworks, Bank Holiday crowds and, from 1895, the Cup Final.
text: The book quotes an observer at dusk at the Crystal Palace: crowds pouring onto the galleries for the fireworks, girls linked arm-in-arm leaping 'like grotesque maenads', fights, drunkenness and lovers whispering 'in a space of five square yards'. The passage is from George Gissing's The Nether World.

The Palace's Saturday concerts, the book notes, started in 1855 a tradition the Proms continued. The Sabbatarians fought to keep it shut on Sundays. From 1895 the FA Cup final was played in its grounds, and the book quotes The Times's leader on the 1899 final.
events: First FA Cup final at the Crystal Palace.

places.name: Zoological Gardens: Jumbo
places.summary: Home of Jumbo, the African elephant whose sale to Barnum in 1882 caused a national uproar.
text: The book gives Jumbo a full chapter. He carried children on his back for years. When the Zoological Society sold him to P. T. Barnum for £2,000 in 1882 because of his temper in his house, Jumbo refused to enter his travelling crate and lay down in the street at the zoo gates, trumpeting to his 'little wife' Alice.

'All England seemed to run mad', Barnum wrote, and Jumbo hats, cigars, collars and polkas sold by the thousand. Letters to The Times proposed buying him back, and the American minister joked that Jumbo was 'the only burning question between England and America'. Jumbo arrived in New York on 9 April 1882 and was killed by a train in Ontario in 1885.
events: Jumbo refuses to leave the Zoo.

places.name: Royal Agricultural Hall
places.summary: Islington's great iron hall for shows and races: in 1887, horse against penny-farthing.
text: The book reproduces the Illustrated London News's picture of a race between a horse and a penny-farthing at the Agricultural Hall in 1887. The hall staged cattle shows, walking matches, circuses and the World's Fair at Christmas.
Bicycle racing, the book notes, soon turned professional and 'ceased to be an amateur sport', a small case of the commercialisation of sport the chapter describes.

images.caption: The World's Fair at the Royal Agricultural Hall, Islington, 1881
images.author: Agricultural Hall World's Fair

places.name: National Sporting Club
places.summary: Founded in 1891 to make boxing respectable under the Queensberry Rules.
text: The book explains that prize-fighting was 'basically illegal and notoriously corrupt' until 1892, with fights held at secret venues reached by special trains. The rules that tamed it were drafted by John Graham Chambers and 'promoted under' the name of the Marquess of Queensberry.

The National Sporting Club, 'upper-middle-class and respectable', replaced the Bohemian Pelican Club in 1891. In 1892 'Gentleman Jim' Corbett beat John L. Sullivan under Queensberry Rules. The man whose name stood for sportsmanship was the man who hounded Wilde.

images.caption: An audience at the National Sporting Club, 1897
images.author: Charles Dana Gibson

places.name: Romano's
places.summary: 'The Roman's' Strand restaurant, favourite of the Gaiety Girls, stage-door johnnies and sporting journalists.
text: The book names Romano's among the fashionable, 'often Bohemian' café-restaurants of Wilde's London, with Verrey's, Gatti's and the Café Royal. Alfonso Nicolino Romano's restaurant was a short walk from the Gaiety, and its suppers were part of the musical-comedy world of George Edwardes.
The book argues that the new restaurants allowed respectable women to dine in public, which helped change the social geography of the West End.

places.name: Gatti's
places.address: Villiers Street and the Strand (Adelaide Gallery)
places.summary: The Swiss Gatti brothers' popular cafés and their 'Gatti's under the Arches' music hall.
text: The book names 'the very popular establishment run by the Gatti brothers' as one of the first great café-restaurants. The Swiss-Italian Gattis ran cafés, ice-cream businesses and music halls, including 'Gatti's in the Arches' under Charing Cross station, and the Adelphi and Vaudeville theatres.
Their success was part of the 'cosmopolitan' London of foreign restaurateurs that Judith Walkowitz has traced in Soho and the Strand.

images.caption: Walter Sickert, Gatti's Hungerford Palace of Varieties: Second Turn of Katie Lawrence, 1888
images.author: Walter Sickert

places.name: Verrey's
places.summary: The Swiss café on Regent Street that the book calls the first well-known café-restaurant.
text: 'The first well-known example' of the café-restaurant, the book says, 'was Verrey's'. Founded by a Swiss confectioner, it served French food and ices to shoppers and theatregoers on Regent Street.

With the Café Royal down the street, it made Regent Street a place where men and women could eat in public. That was new, and the book notes the guidebooks' advice to unescorted ladies about which doors to avoid.

places.name: Royalty Theatre: the Independent Theatre
places.summary: Where J. T. Grein's Independent Theatre staged Ibsen's Ghosts (1891) and Shaw's first play, Widowers' Houses (1892).
text: The Independent Theatre Society used private subscription performances to get around the Lord Chamberlain's censor. Its first production, Ghosts, on 13 March 1891, set off the critics' fury the book quotes from Clement Scott: 'The playhouse is not a charnel house; the drama is not a dissecting knife.'
In December 1892 it staged Shaw's Widowers' Houses, a play about slum landlords. The book says it 'created a furor... in part, no doubt, because it was a bad play', and dates it to 1893.

images.caption: Royalty Theatre, Dean Street, playbill c. 1890
images.author: Hardy, Dudley (Sheffield, 15–01–1867 - Londres, 11–08–1922), dessinateur

places.name: Avenue Theatre: Arms and the Man
places.summary: Florence Farr's 1894 season, paid for by Annie Horniman, brought Shaw's Arms and the Man and Yeats's first staged play.
text: The book calls Arms and the Man 'a play delightfully subversive in its easygoing satire of Victorian melodramatic conventions'. It opened here on 21 April 1894, in the actress Florence Farr's season, funded anonymously by the tea heiress Annie Horniman. The curtain-raiser was Yeats's The Land of Heart's Desire.
The book argues that Shaw learned the satirical touch from 'Wilde's world of words in the service of social criticism'. Farr and Horniman were both members of the Golden Dawn, like Constance Wilde.

images.caption: The Playhouse (formerly the Avenue Theatre), Northumberland Avenue
images.author: PAUL FARMER

places.name: St James's Hall
places.summary: London's principal concert hall before the Queen's Hall, and home of the Moore and Burgess Minstrels.
text: The great hall hosted the Monday Popular Concerts and Dickens's public readings, while in the smaller hall below the Moore and Burgess Minstrels played for decades. The book's account of music-hall song includes the blackface 'coon' songs of Eugene Stratton, who 'often came to the music hall stage from the minstrel troupes'. Stratton came from Moore and Burgess.
The hall linked the 'serious' and popular music the book describes, and its demolition in 1905 coincided with the rise of Henry Wood's Queen's Hall.

places.name: The Crown, Charing Cross Road
places.summary: The decadents' pub, where Dowson, Johnson, Symons and Beardsley drank after the music halls closed.
text: In the 1890s the Crown's back parlour was where the Rhymers and the Yellow Book set gathered late at night after the Empire and the Alhambra had emptied. Dowson, Lionel Johnson, Arthur Symons and the young Beardsley were regulars.

The book quotes Holbrook Jackson on the dilettanti who drank absinthe 'and discussed its "cloudy green" suggestiveness'. The Crown was a cheaper version of the Café Royal, where young poets went to look at one another.

places.name: Thames Ironworks, Canning Town
places.summary: The shipyard that built ironclads and whose works team, founded in 1895, became West Ham United.
text: The book lists the workplace as one of the sources of football clubs, with 'the (Woolwich) Arsenal and West Ham United (originally called Thames Ironworks after the shipyard) being the most famous'. The yard's owner, Arnold Hills, founded the works team in 1895 to improve relations after a strike.
The yard built warships for the Admiralty and foreign navies. It is a reminder of the industrial East End beyond the docks, the London of heavy industry the book says the capital mostly lacked.
events: Thames Ironworks FC founded (later West Ham United).

images.caption: Building HMS Warrior at the Thames Ironworks, 1860
images.author: Edwin Weedon

places.name: Whitechapel Road: the 'Elephant Man'
places.address: Whitechapel Road, opposite the London Hospital
places.summary: Joseph Merrick was exhibited in a shop here in 1884, and lived in the London Hospital opposite until his death in 1890.
text: The book's chapter on diversions describes the shows of 'unusual or freakish people' that went with circuses and fairs, from Tom Thumb at Buckingham Palace to a travelling dwarf who prodded the animals. In November 1884 the surgeon Frederick Treves paid to see Joseph Merrick, displayed as 'the Elephant Man' in an empty shop on the Whitechapel Road.

After the police closed such shows, Merrick was found destitute and given rooms in the London Hospital, where society visitors, including the Princess of Wales, came to see him. He died there in April 1890. His story shows how the freak show, philanthropy and medicine overlapped.
events: Treves sees Merrick exhibited on Whitechapel Road.
Joseph Merrick dies at the London Hospital.

places.name: London Bridge and the Pool of London
places.summary: The river was London's 'silent highway': barges, steamers and the Hamburg boats bringing immigrants upstream.
text: The book reproduces a Kodak view of the Thames in 1901 as London's 'silent highway' and lifeline, 'bringing in raw materials and shipping out finished goods to the new empire', with industry and slums along both banks. It sets J. W. Thompson's photograph of bargemen beside it: their work was 'unsteady and wages often below the minimum needed for survival'.

Below London Bridge, in the Pool, the Hamburg boats anchored and immigrants were rowed ashore, as Beatrice Potter described. Crowded steamboats, the book adds, turned the river into a commuter highway.

places.name: The Old Nichol and the Boundary Estate
places.summary: The notorious slum of Arthur Morrison's A Child of the Jago, cleared by the new London County Council for its first great housing estate.
text: The book notes that London had no city government until the first London County Council was elected in 1889, and quotes its chairman Lord Rosebery 'haunted by the awfulness of London'. The LCC's first great act of slum clearance was here, at the Old Nichol in Shoreditch. It began clearing the area in 1890 and built the Boundary Estate around Arnold Circus by 1900.

Arthur Morrison's novel A Child of the Jago (1896) made the Nichol infamous. Few of its residents could afford the new flats, a problem the book raises when it says poverty increased even as conditions improved.
events: LCC resolves to clear the Old Nichol.
A Child of the Jago published.

walks.d: From the triumph of Earnest to the night boat to Dieppe, in twenty stops across London.
stops: 14 February 1895: The Importance of Being Earnest opens. Queensberry is turned away with his vegetables.
18 February: Queensberry leaves his card. Wilde receives it on the 28th.
28 February: from his hotel, Wilde writes to Ross that he must prosecute.
2 March: Queensberry is arrested and charged with criminal libel.
Late March: Frank Harris and Shaw urge Wilde to drop the case and go abroad.
3–5 April: Carson's cross-examination; the prosecution collapses.
5 April: Wilde writes to the Evening News.
Taken to Scotland Yard, then charged.
6 April: bail refused; committal hearings follow.
24 April: the contents of the house are sold.
7 May: out on bail, he is turned out of the Midland.
7 May, late: refuge with his mother, 'a wounded stag'.
May: the Leversons take him in.
25 May: convicted and sentenced to two years' hard labour.
September and November: the bankruptcy court. Ross raises his hat.
20 November: on the platform, in convict dress, on the way to Reading.
The Jesuits say no. That night he leaves for Dieppe.

walks.d: How a penniless Oxford graduate made himself the most talked-about man in London.

The temple of Aestheticism, which Wilde had reviewed at Oxford.

The 'shy artificers of Chelsea', Rossetti and Swinburne.

1883: bachelor rooms after America and Paris.

Salome and The Sphinx; The Yellow Book.

Dinners with young men in Soho.

errata.said: Wilde was sentenced to two years' hard labour 'on May 25, 1889'.
errata.fix: The sentence was passed on 25 May 1895. 1889 is a misprint.

errata.said: The Cleveland Street affair 'first came to light on July 4, 1886'.
errata.fix: The theft that started the inquiry happened in July 1889. The scandal ran from 1889 into 1890.

errata.said: The Rhymers' Club 'gathered at the Cheshire Cheese in the Strand'.
errata.fix: Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese is on Fleet Street, in Wine Office Court.
Seven Dials is in St Giles, beside Covent Garden in the West End.

errata.said: The Bancrofts 'first played and managed the Prince of Wales's Theatre on Coventry Street'.
errata.fix: The Bancrofts' Prince of Wales's was in Tottenham Street. The Coventry Street theatre opened in 1884 and took the name in 1886.

errata.said: The City and South London Railway 'was nicknamed "the two-penny tube"'.
errata.fix: 'Twopenny Tube' was the nickname of the Central London Railway, opened in 1900.

errata.said: A Gaiety Girl 'played the Prince of Wales's Theatre in 1895'.
Shaw's 'Widower's House created a furor in 1893'.
errata.fix: Widowers' Houses opened at the Royalty Theatre in December 1892.

errata.said: Stead 'went to jail for two months'.
errata.fix: Stead was sentenced to three months.

errata.said: Annie Chapman was found 'in back of Dr. Thomas Barnardo's children's asylum'.
errata.fix: She was found in the back yard of a lodging house at 29 Hanbury Street, Spitalfields.

errata.said: 'Wilde lived with Miles from 1879 to 1880' (caption to the design for 1 Tite Street).
errata.fix: They shared 13 Salisbury Street from 1879 and moved to Tite Street in 1880. Wilde left in 1881.

errata.said: Beardsley died 'at the age of twenty-five' (p. 37) and 'at the age of twenty-six' (p. 51).
errata.fix: Beardsley (born August 1872, died March 1898) was twenty-five.

errata.said: Photographs credited to 'J. W. Thompson', including 'The Street Doctor'.
errata.fix: 'The Street Doctor' is from John Thomson's Street Life in London (1877).

errata.said: Charles Parker met Wilde at 'a restaurant in Rupert Street. I think it was the Solferino.'
errata.fix: This is not exactly an error, but the sources disagree. Press reports of the libel trial have Wilde saying he first met Parker at Kettner's, and William Parker said the same at the second trial.
